declarations.name: TarskiQueryTree
declarations.informal: A deterministic adaptive query algorithm for an unknown map f : [n]^k → [n]^k, as a decision tree: a leaf outputs a point; an internal node queries f at a point x and continues according to the value f(x).
declarations.statement: inductive TarskiQueryTree (n k : ℕ)
declarations.source:
/-- A deterministic adaptive query algorithm for a black-box map `[n]^k → [n]^k`, as a decision tree: a leaf outputs a point; an internal node queries the map at a point and branches on the returned value. -/
inductive TarskiQueryTree (n k : ℕ) | output : (Fin k → Fin n) → TarskiQueryTree n k
  | query : (Fin k → Fin n) → ((Fin k → Fin n) → TarskiQueryTree n k) → TarskiQueryTree n k
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07055 (Tarski fixed points in quasi-FPT queries), Sec. 1 (the black-box query model; deterministic algorithms as decision trees)

declarations.name: spr_sign_count
declarations.informal: The number of signs on a board of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game with n cells, each empty or holding a plus or a minus.
declarations.statement: def spr_sign_count {n : ℕ} (b : Fin n → Option Bool) : ℕ
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07623 (Explicit asymptotic bounds for sequential calibration beyond T^{2/3}), Sec. 2.2 (payoff of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game)

declarations.name: spr_move
declarations.informal: The board after the labeler empties the cells of a set R and places the sign s in the selected cell j.
declarations.statement:
def spr_move {n : ℕ} (b : Fin n → Option Bool) (j : Fin n) (R : Finset (Fin n)) (s : Bool) :
    Fin n → Option Bool
declarations.source:
/-- The board after the labeler empties the cells of `R` and places sign `s` in cell `j`. -/
def spr_move {n : ℕ} (b : Fin n → Option Bool) (j : Fin n) (R : Finset (Fin n)) (s : Bool) :
    Fin n → Option Bool :=
  fun i => if i = j then some s else if i ∈ R then none else b i
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07623 (Explicit asymptotic bounds for sequential calibration beyond T^{2/3}), Sec. 2.2, steps 2-3 of a round

declarations.name: TarskiQueryTree.run
declarations.informal: The point a query tree outputs when the black box is f.
declarations.statement:
def TarskiQueryTree.run {n k : ℕ} (f : (Fin k → Fin n) → (Fin k → Fin n)) :
    TarskiQueryTree n k → (Fin k → Fin n)
declarations.source:
/-- The point a query tree outputs when the black box is `f`. -/
def TarskiQueryTree.run {n k : ℕ} (f : (Fin k → Fin n) → (Fin k → Fin n)) :
    TarskiQueryTree n k → (Fin k → Fin n) := fun
  | .output x => x
  | .query x next => (next (f x)).run f
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07055 (Tarski fixed points in quasi-FPT queries), Sec. 1

declarations.name: TarskiQueryTree.cost
declarations.informal: The number of queries a query tree makes when the black box is f (the length of the path f follows).
declarations.statement:
def TarskiQueryTree.cost {n k : ℕ} (f : (Fin k → Fin n) → (Fin k → Fin n)) :
    TarskiQueryTree n k → ℕ
declarations.source:
/-- The number of queries a query tree makes when the black box is `f`. -/
def TarskiQueryTree.cost {n k : ℕ} (f : (Fin k → Fin n) → (Fin k → Fin n)) :
    TarskiQueryTree n k → ℕ := fun
  | .output _ => 0
  | .query x next => (next (f x)).cost f + 1
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07055 (Tarski fixed points in quasi-FPT queries), Sec. 1

declarations.name: tarski_query_complexity_le
declarations.informal: Tarski(n, k) ≤ q: some deterministic query algorithm finds a fixed point of every monotone map f : [n]^k → [n]^k (componentwise order) using at most q queries.
declarations.statement: def tarski_query_complexity_le (n k q : ℕ) : Prop
declarations.source:
/-- `Tarski(n, k) ≤ q`: some deterministic query algorithm finds a fixed point of every monotone map `f : [n]^k → [n]^k` (componentwise order) with at most `q` queries. -/
def tarski_query_complexity_le (n k q : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ t : TarskiQueryTree n k, ∀ f : (Fin k → Fin n) → (Fin k → Fin n), Monotone f →
    f (t.run f) = t.run f ∧ t.cost f ≤ q
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07055 (Tarski fixed points in quasi-FPT queries), Sec. 1 (deterministic query complexity of Tarski(n, k)); the grid is {0, …, n−1}^k instead of {1, …, n}^k

declarations.name: spr_value
declarations.informal: The minimax value of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game with r rounds left from a given board: the pointer (maximizer) may stop or select an empty cell j; the labeler (minimizer) then removes any subset of the minus signs to the left of j and the plus signs to the right of j and places a plus or minus in j; the game ends when the pointer stops, the rounds run out, or no cell is empty, and the payoff is the number of signs on the board.
declarations.statement: def spr_value (n : ℕ) : ℕ → (Fin n → Option Bool) → ℕ
declarations.source:
/-- Value of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game with `r` rounds left from board `b`, under optimal play: the pointer (maximizer) may stop, or select an empty cell `j`; the labeler (minimizer) then empties any legal set `R` (minus signs left of `j`, plus signs right of `j`) and places a sign in `j`. The game ends when the pointer stops, no rounds are left, or no cell is empty; the payoff is the number of signs on the board. -/
def spr_value (n : ℕ) : ℕ → (Fin n → Option Bool) → ℕ := fun
  | 0, b => spr_sign_count b
  | r + 1, b =>
    max (spr_sign_count b)
      ((Finset.univ.filter fun j => b j = none).sup fun j =>
        ((Finset.univ : Finset (Finset (Fin n) × Bool)).filter
            fun p => ∀ i ∈ p.1, (i < j ∧ b i = some false) ∨ (j < i ∧ b i = some true)).inf'
          ⟨(∅, true), Finset.mem_filter.2
            ⟨Finset.mem_univ _, fun i hi => absurd hi (Finset.notMem_empty i)⟩⟩
          fun p => spr_value n r (spr_move b j p.1 p.2))
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07623 (Explicit asymptotic bounds for sequential calibration beyond T^{2/3}), Sec. 2.2 (the game is one of perfect information, so the value with randomized strategies equals this pure minimax value)

declarations.name: spr_opt
declarations.informal: opt(n, t): the number of signs remaining at the end of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game with n cells and at most t rounds, under optimal play, starting from the empty board.
declarations.statement: def spr_opt (n t : ℕ) : ℕ
declarations.source:
/-- `opt(n, t)`: the number of signs remaining at the end of the sign-preservation-with-reuse game with `n` cells and at most `t` rounds, starting from the empty board, under optimal play. -/
def spr_opt (n t : ℕ) : ℕ := spr_value n t fun _ => none
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07623 (Explicit asymptotic bounds for sequential calibration beyond T^{2/3}), Sec. 2.2 (definition of opt(n, t))

declarations.name: not_matroid_common_colorable_loopyOn_zero
declarations.informal: A nonempty ground set has no common coloring with zero colors.
declarations.statement:
theorem not_matroid_common_colorable_loopyOn_zero {α : Type*} (a : α) :
    ¬ matroid_common_colorable (Matroid.loopyOn {a}) (Matroid.loopyOn {a}) 0
declarations.source:
theorem not_matroid_common_colorable_loopyOn_zero {α : Type*} (a : α) :
    ¬ matroid_common_colorable (Matroid.loopyOn {a}) (Matroid.loopyOn {a}) 0 := by
  intro ⟨c, hc, _⟩
  have ha : a ∈ (Matroid.loopyOn ({a} : Set α)).E := by
    rw [Matroid.loopyOn_ground]
    exact Set.mem_singleton a
  exact Nat.not_lt_zero _ (hc a ha)

explanation.summary: The proof argues by contradiction. If a common 0-coloring existed for the loopy matroid on {a}, each element in its ground set would be assigned a natural number color strictly less than 0. But a belongs to the ground set {a}, and no natural number is strictly less than 0.

steps.claim: Assume for contradiction that a common 0-coloring exists.
steps.explanation: By the definition of a common matroid coloring with 0 colors, there would exist a coloring function c : α → ℕ such that every element e in the ground set of the first matroid satisfies c(e) < 0.
steps.code: intro ⟨c, hc, _⟩

steps.claim: The element a belongs to the ground set of the loopy matroid on {a}.
steps.explanation: By Matroid.loopyOn_ground, the ground set of Matroid.loopyOn {a} is the set {a}, which contains a by Set.mem_singleton.
steps.code:
have ha : a ∈ (Matroid.loopyOn ({a} : Set α)).E := by
    rw [Matroid.loopyOn_ground]
    exact Set.mem_singleton a

steps.claim: This leads to a contradiction.
steps.explanation: Applying the coloring property to the element a gives c(a) < 0. However, Nat.not_lt_zero states that no natural number is strictly less than 0, yielding a contradiction.
steps.code: exact Nat.not_lt_zero _ (hc a ha)

glossary.Matroid.loopyOn_ground: The ground set of a loopy matroid on E is E itself.
glossary.Set.mem_singleton: For any element a, a is in the singleton set {a}.
glossary.Nat.not_lt_zero: No natural number is strictly less than zero.

declarations.name: multilinear_extension_indicator
declarations.informal: The multilinear extension agrees with f on indicator vectors: F(1_S) = f(S).
declarations.statement:
theorem multilinear_extension_indicator {m : ℕ} (f : Finset (Fin m) → ℝ) (S : Finset (Fin m)) :
    multilinear_extension f (finset_indicator_vec S) = f S
declarations.source:
theorem multilinear_extension_indicator {m : ℕ} (f : Finset (Fin m) → ℝ) (S : Finset (Fin m)) :
    multilinear_extension f (finset_indicator_vec S) = f S := by
  dsimp [multilinear_extension]
  rw [Finset.sum_eq_single_of_mem S (Finset.mem_univ S)]
  · have h1 : (∏ u ∈ S, finset_indicator_vec S u) = 1 := by
      apply Finset.prod_eq_one
      intro u hu
      dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
      rw [if_pos hu]
    have h2 : (∏ u ∈ Sᶜ, (1 - finset_indicator_vec S u)) = 1 := by
      apply Finset.prod_eq_one
      intro u hu
      have hu' : u ∉ S := by
        rw [Finset.mem_compl] at hu
        exact hu
      dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
      rw [if_neg hu']
      ring
    rw [h1, h2, mul_one, mul_one]
  · intro T _ hne
    have hdisj : (∃ u ∈ T, u ∉ S) ∨ (∃ u ∈ S, u ∉ T) := by
      by_contra! h
      rcases h with ⟨h1, h2⟩
      exact hne (Finset.Subset.antisymm h1 h2)
    cases hdisj with
    | inl h1 =>
      rcases h1 with ⟨u, huT, huS⟩
      have hzero : ∏ u ∈ T, finset_indicator_vec S u = 0 := by
        apply Finset.prod_eq_zero huT
        dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
        rw [if_neg huS]
      rw [hzero, mul_zero, zero_mul]
    | inr h2 =>
      rcases h2 with ⟨u, huS, huT⟩
      have hucompl : u ∈ Tᶜ := by
        rw [Finset.mem_compl]
        exact huT
      have hzero : ∏ u ∈ Tᶜ, (1 - finset_indicator_vec S u) = 0 := by
        apply Finset.prod_eq_zero hucompl
        dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
        rw [if_pos huS]
        ring
      rw [hzero, mul_zero]

explanation.summary: The multilinear extension of a function f is defined as a sum over all subsets T of {0, ..., m-1}. By isolating the term T = S using `Finset.sum_eq_single_of_mem`, the proof reduces to showing that the summand at S evaluates to f(S) and all other summands vanish. For T = S, both products evaluate to 1 because 1_S(u) = 1 on S and 1_S(u) = 0 on Sᶜ. For any T ≠ S, either some element lies in T ∖ S (making the first product zero) or some element lies in S ∖ T (making the second product zero), so every other term is zero.

steps.claim: The multilinear extension sum reduces to evaluating the summand for T = S and showing that every summand for T ≠ S vanishes.
steps.explanation: Unfolding the definition of `multilinear_extension` expresses the value as a sum over all subsets. Applying `Finset.sum_eq_single_of_mem` with S ∈ Finset.univ isolates the single term T = S, leaving two obligations: proving the term for T = S equals f(S), and proving every term for T ≠ S is zero.
steps.code:
dsimp [multilinear_extension]
  rw [Finset.sum_eq_single_of_mem S (Finset.mem_univ S)]

steps.claim: The product ∏ u ∈ S, 1_S(u) equals 1.
steps.explanation: For each u ∈ S, the indicator function 1_S(u) evaluates to 1 by `if_pos`. By `Finset.prod_eq_one`, since every factor in the product over S is 1, the entire product equals 1.
steps.code:
· have h1 : (∏ u ∈ S, finset_indicator_vec S u) = 1 := by
      apply Finset.prod_eq_one
      intro u hu
      dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
      rw [if_pos hu]

steps.claim: The product ∏ u ∈ Sᶜ, (1 - 1_S(u)) equals 1.
steps.explanation: For each u ∈ Sᶜ, we have u ∉ S by `Finset.mem_compl`, so the indicator 1_S(u) evaluates to 0 by `if_neg`. Each factor is therefore 1 - 0 = 1, and by `Finset.prod_eq_one`, the product over Sᶜ equals 1.
steps.code:
have h2 : (∏ u ∈ Sᶜ, (1 - finset_indicator_vec S u)) = 1 := by
      apply Finset.prod_eq_one
      intro u hu
      have hu' : u ∉ S := by
        rw [Finset.mem_compl] at hu
        exact hu
      dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
      rw [if_neg hu']
      ring

steps.claim: The summand for T = S simplifies to f(S).
steps.explanation: Substituting the values of the two products (both equal to 1) into (f(S) * 1) * 1 and simplifying with `mul_one` shows that the summand at S is f(S).
steps.code: rw [h1, h2, mul_one, mul_one]

steps.claim: If T ≠ S, then either there is some element in T ∖ S or some element in S ∖ T.
steps.explanation: Proceeding by contradiction, if neither condition held, then every element of T would be in S and every element of S in T (that is, T ⊆ S and S ⊆ T). By `Finset.Subset.antisymm`, this would mean T = S, contradicting T ≠ S.
steps.code:
· intro T _ hne
    have hdisj : (∃ u ∈ T, u ∉ S) ∨ (∃ u ∈ S, u ∉ T) := by
      by_contra! h
      rcases h with ⟨h1, h2⟩
      exact hne (Finset.Subset.antisymm h1 h2)

steps.claim: If there is an element u ∈ T ∖ S, the summand for T is 0.
steps.explanation: Since u ∉ S, the indicator 1_S(u) is 0 by `if_neg`. Because u ∈ T, `Finset.prod_eq_zero` implies that the product ∏ x ∈ T, 1_S(x) has a zero factor and vanishes. Multiplying by zero (`mul_zero`, `zero_mul`) makes the entire summand 0.
steps.code:
cases hdisj with
    | inl h1 =>
      rcases h1 with ⟨u, huT, huS⟩
      have hzero : ∏ u ∈ T, finset_indicator_vec S u = 0 := by
        apply Finset.prod_eq_zero huT
        dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
        rw [if_neg huS]
      rw [hzero, mul_zero, zero_mul]

steps.claim: If there is an element u ∈ S ∖ T, the summand for T is 0.
steps.explanation: Since u ∉ T, u ∈ Tᶜ by `Finset.mem_compl`. Since u ∈ S, 1_S(u) is 1 by `if_pos`, so the factor 1 - 1_S(u) is 0. Because u ∈ Tᶜ, `Finset.prod_eq_zero` shows that the product ∏ x ∈ Tᶜ, (1 - 1_S(x)) vanishes. Multiplying by zero (`mul_zero`) makes the entire summand 0.
steps.code:
| inr h2 =>
      rcases h2 with ⟨u, huS, huT⟩
      have hucompl : u ∈ Tᶜ := by
        rw [Finset.mem_compl]
        exact huT
      have hzero : ∏ u ∈ Tᶜ, (1 - finset_indicator_vec S u) = 0 := by
        apply Finset.prod_eq_zero hucompl
        dsimp [finset_indicator_vec]
        rw [if_pos huS]
        ring
      rw [hzero, mul_zero]

glossary.Finset.sum_eq_single_of_mem: If every element of a finite set except possibly a designated element has value 0, the sum over the set equals the value at that element.
glossary.Finset.mem_univ: Every element of a finite type belongs to the universal finset `Finset.univ`.
glossary.Finset.prod_eq_one: If every factor in a finite product equals 1, the product equals 1.
glossary.Finset.mem_compl: An element belongs to the complement of a finset if and only if it does not belong to the finset.
glossary.Finset.Subset.antisymm: Two finite sets that are subsets of each other are equal.
glossary.Finset.prod_eq_zero: If at least one factor in a finite product is 0, the product equals 0.
glossary.if_pos: If the condition of an if-then-else expression holds, the expression evaluates to the 'then' branch.
glossary.if_neg: If the condition of an if-then-else expression is false, the expression evaluates to the 'else' branch.
glossary.mul_one: Multiplying any element by 1 on the right yields the element itself (a * 1 = a).
glossary.mul_zero: Multiplying any element by 0 on the right yields 0 (a * 0 = 0).
glossary.zero_mul: Multiplying any element by 0 on the left yields 0 (0 * a = 0).

declarations.name: linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le
declarations.informal: If rank L(x ⊗ y ⊗ z) ≤ ρ for all x, y, z, then rank L(T) ≤ r ρ for every sum T of r pure tensors; this is why potency greater than r yields equations for tensors of rank at most r.
declarations.statement:
theorem linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le {n u v : ℕ}
    (L : (Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℂ) →ₗ[ℂ] Matrix (Fin u) (Fin v) ℂ) (ρ : ℕ)
    (hρ : ∀ x y z : Fin n → ℂ, (L (tensor3_pure x y z)).rank ≤ ρ)
    (r : ℕ) (x y z : Fin r → Fin n → ℂ) :
    (L (∑ i, tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank ≤ r * ρ
declarations.source:
lemma linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_add {u v : ℕ} (A B : Matrix (Fin u) (Fin v) ℂ) :
    (A + B).rank ≤ A.rank + B.rank := by
  dsimp [Matrix.rank]
  rw [Matrix.mulVecLin_add]
  have h_le : LinearMap.range (Matrix.mulVecLin A + Matrix.mulVecLin B) ≤
      LinearMap.range (Matrix.mulVecLin A) ⊔ LinearMap.range (Matrix.mulVecLin B) :=
    LinearMap.range_add_le _ _
  have h_mono := Submodule.finrank_mono h_le
  exact h_mono.trans (Submodule.finrank_add_le_finrank_add_finrank _ _)

lemma linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_sum {ι : Type*} {u v : ℕ}
    (s : Finset ι) (F : ι → Matrix (Fin u) (Fin v) ℂ) :
    (∑ i ∈ s, F i).rank ≤ ∑ i ∈ s, (F i).rank := by
  induction s using Finset.cons_induction with
  | empty =>
    simp
  | cons a s ha ih =>
    rw [Finset.sum_cons, Finset.sum_cons]
    have h_add := linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_add (F a) (∑ i ∈ s, F i)
    exact h_add.trans (Nat.add_le_add_left ih _)

theorem linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le {n u v : ℕ}
    (L : (Fin n → Fin n → Fin n → ℂ) →ₗ[ℂ] Matrix (Fin u) (Fin v) ℂ) (ρ : ℕ)
    (hρ : ∀ x y z : Fin n → ℂ, (L (tensor3_pure x y z)).rank ≤ ρ)
    (r : ℕ) (x y z : Fin r → Fin n → ℂ) :
    (L (∑ i, tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank ≤ r * ρ := by
  rw [map_sum]
  have h1 : (∑ i, L (tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank ≤
      ∑ i, (L (tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank :=
    linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_sum Finset.univ _
  have h2 : ∑ i : Fin r, (L (tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank ≤
      ∑ _i : Fin r, ρ :=
    Finset.sum_le_sum (fun i _ => hρ (x i) (y i) (z i))
  rw [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_fin, nsmul_eq_mul] at h2
  exact h1.trans h2
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.08504 (Explicit tensors beyond the linear flattening barrier), Sec. 1 (the linear flattening method: Pot(L) > r gives nontrivial equations for σ_r); rank version, without the closure step to border rank

explanation.summary: The theorem is proved by combining the subadditivity of matrix rank with the linearity of L. First, matrix rank is subadditive under addition, which extends by finite induction to show that the rank of any finite sum of matrices is bounded by the sum of their individual ranks. Applying linearity distributes L over the sum of r pure tensors, expressing L(T) as a sum of r matrices. Since each pure tensor has image rank at most ρ by hypothesis, subadditivity bounds the total rank by the sum of these r bounds, which evaluates to r * ρ.

steps.claim: For any two matrices A and B, rank(A + B) ≤ rank(A) + rank(B).
steps.explanation: Unfolding the definition of rank (Matrix.rank) as the dimension of the range of the associated linear map and rewriting the map of a sum as the sum of maps (Matrix.mulVecLin_add), the range of the sum is contained in the span of the ranges by LinearMap.range_add_le. By monotonicity of subspace dimension (Submodule.finrank_mono), the rank of A + B is at most the dimension of this span, which by Submodule.finrank_add_le_finrank_add_finrank is bounded by the sum of the individual ranks.
steps.code:
dsimp [Matrix.rank]
  rw [Matrix.mulVecLin_add]
  have h_le : LinearMap.range (Matrix.mulVecLin A + Matrix.mulVecLin B) ≤
      LinearMap.range (Matrix.mulVecLin A) ⊔ LinearMap.range (Matrix.mulVecLin B) :=
    LinearMap.range_add_le _ _
  have h_mono := Submodule.finrank_mono h_le
  exact h_mono.trans (Submodule.finrank_add_le_finrank_add_finrank _ _)

steps.claim: For any finite set s and family of matrices F, rank(∑_{i ∈ s} F i) ≤ ∑_{i ∈ s} rank(F i).
steps.explanation: We proceed by induction on the finite set s using Finset.cons_induction. For the empty set s = ∅, both sides evaluate to zero. For the inductive step s ∪ {a} with a ∉ s, we split off the term F(a) using Finset.sum_cons, apply two-matrix subadditivity (linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_add) to F(a) + ∑_{i ∈ s} F(i), and invoke the induction hypothesis via Nat.add_le_add_left.
steps.code:
induction s using Finset.cons_induction with
  | empty =>
    simp
  | cons a s ha ih =>
    rw [Finset.sum_cons, Finset.sum_cons]
    have h_add := linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_add (F a) (∑ i ∈ s, F i)
    exact h_add.trans (Nat.add_le_add_left ih _)

steps.claim: The rank of L(∑_{i=1}^r x_i ⊗ y_i ⊗ z_i) is bounded by the sum of ranks ∑_{i=1}^r rank(L(x_i ⊗ y_i ⊗ z_i)).
steps.explanation: By linearity of L (map_sum), L distributes over the sum of pure tensors. Applying the finite subadditivity lemma (linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_sum) over the full index set Finset.univ bounds the rank of this matrix sum by the sum of the ranks of each term.
steps.code:
rw [map_sum]
  have h1 : (∑ i, L (tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank ≤
      ∑ i, (L (tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank :=
    linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_sum Finset.univ _

steps.claim: The sum of ranks ∑_{i=1}^r rank(L(x_i ⊗ y_i ⊗ z_i)) is at most r * ρ.
steps.explanation: By hypothesis hρ, each pure tensor satisfies rank(L(x_i ⊗ y_i ⊗ z_i)) ≤ ρ. Summing these bounds over Fin r via Finset.sum_le_sum gives the sum of the constant ρ over Fin r. Applying Finset.sum_const, evaluating the cardinality of Fin r as r via Finset.card_fin, and converting natural scalar multiplication to ordinary multiplication via nsmul_eq_mul simplifies this bound to r * ρ.
steps.code:
have h2 : ∑ i : Fin r, (L (tensor3_pure (x i) (y i) (z i))).rank ≤
      ∑ _i : Fin r, ρ :=
    Finset.sum_le_sum (fun i _ => hρ (x i) (y i) (z i))
  rw [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_fin, nsmul_eq_mul] at h2

steps.claim: The rank of L(∑_{i=1}^r x_i ⊗ y_i ⊗ z_i) is at most r * ρ.
steps.explanation: Combining the subadditivity bound from the third step with the rank bound on the sum from the fourth step by transitivity of inequality concludes the proof.
steps.code: exact h1.trans h2

glossary.Matrix.rank: The rank of a matrix is the dimension (finrank) of the range of its associated linear map.
glossary.Matrix.mulVecLin_add: The linear map associated with the sum of two matrices is the sum of the linear maps associated with each matrix.
glossary.LinearMap.range_add_le: The range of the sum of two linear maps is contained in the join (sum of submodules) of their individual ranges.
glossary.Submodule.finrank_mono: Submodule dimension is monotonic with respect to inclusion: if s ≤ t, then the dimension of s is at most the dimension of t.
glossary.Submodule.finrank_add_le_finrank_add_fin: The dimension of the join of two submodules is at most the sum of their individual dimensions.
glossary.Finset.cons_induction: Induction principle for finite sets: a property holds for all finite sets if it holds for the empty set and is preserved when inserting a new element.
glossary.Finset.sum_cons: The sum of a function over a finite set with a new element inserted equals the value at that element plus the sum over the original set.
glossary.linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_: The rank of the sum of two complex matrices is at most the sum of their individual ranks.
glossary.Nat.add_le_add_left: Adding a fixed natural number to the left of both sides of an inequality preserves the inequality.
glossary.map_sum: A linear map preserves finite sums, mapping the sum of elements to the sum of their images.
glossary.linear_flattening_rank_sum_pure_le_rank_: The rank of a finite sum of complex matrices is at most the sum of their individual ranks.
glossary.Finset.sum_le_sum: If each term in a finite sum is bounded by the corresponding term in another sum, the total sum is bounded by the second sum.
glossary.Finset.sum_const: The sum of a constant value over a finite set equals the cardinality of the set scalar-multiplied by that constant.
glossary.Finset.card_fin: The cardinality of the universal set of type Fin n is n.
glossary.nsmul_eq_mul: Scalar multiplication of an element by a natural number equals ordinary multiplication by that natural number in a semiring.

caveats: In step 2 (line 16), the base case for the empty set is handled by the `simp` tactic, which automatically evaluates empty sums to zero and proves 0 ≤ 0.
In step 4 (line 34), scalar multiplication by a natural number (r • ρ) arising from Finset.sum_const is formally rewritten to standard multiplication (r * ρ) via nsmul_eq_mul.

declarations.name: spr_opt_two_two
declarations.informal: opt(2, 2) = 1: on two cells with two rounds, the labeler can keep at most one sign on the board.
declarations.statement: theorem spr_opt_two_two : spr_opt 2 2 = 1
declarations.source: theorem spr_opt_two_two : spr_opt 2 2 = 1 := rfl
declarations.citation: smallest nontrivial case of opt(n, n) for the sign-preservation-with-reuse game of arXiv:2610.07623 (Sec. 2.2); computed exhaustively

explanation.summary: The theorem asserts that on a board of two cells over two rounds, the optimal number of signs the labeler can secure is 1. Because the board size and round count are small and finite, Lean computes the minimax value directly through definitional reduction. The equality holds by reflexivity (`rfl`).

steps.claim: spr_opt 2 2 = 1
steps.explanation: The game is played on n = 2 cells over t = 2 rounds. In round 1, placing a sign on either cell leaves the other empty. In round 2, playing the remaining empty cell allows the adversary to erase the previously placed sign, so no strategy can achieve more than 1 sign on the board. declarations.name: catch_up_outcome_neg_eq_loss_iff
declarations.informal: Negating a Catch-Up outcome yields a loss if and only if the original outcome is a win.
declarations.statement:
theorem catch_up_outcome_neg_eq_loss_iff (o : CatchUpOutcome) :
    o.neg = CatchUpOutcome.loss ↔ o = CatchUpOutcome.win
declarations.source:
/-- Negating a Catch-Up outcome yields a loss if and only if the original outcome was a win. -/
theorem catch_up_outcome_neg_eq_loss_iff (o : CatchUpOutcome) :
    o.neg = CatchUpOutcome.loss ↔ o = CatchUpOutcome.win := by
  cases o <;> simp [CatchUpOutcome.neg]
declarations.reading: For every `o : CatchUpOutcome`, `CatchUpOutcome.neg o` equals `CatchUpOutcome.loss` if and only if `o` equals `CatchUpOutcome.win`.

explanation.summary: The proof proceeds by exhaustively checking the three constructors of CatchUpOutcome (win, loss, and draw). In each case, unfolding the definition of outcome negation simplifies both sides of the equivalence to identical truth values, closing the goal.

steps.claim: For every outcome o, o.neg = loss if and only if o = win.
steps.explanation: We split into cases on the three possible values of o (win, loss, and draw). In each case, simplifying with the definition of CatchUpOutcome.neg evaluates the negation: win.neg becomes loss (yielding true ↔ true), loss.neg becomes win (yielding false ↔ false), and draw.neg becomes draw (yielding false ↔ false). The simplifier closes each trivial equivalence.
steps.code: cases o <;> simp [CatchUpOutcome.neg]

declarations.name: catch_up_value_eq_loss_iff
declarations.informal: For any nonempty finite set S of natural numbers, the game value catch_up_value S is CatchUpOutcome.loss if and only if for every element x ∈ S, the second player wins from the resulting position, i.e., catch_up_value_aux (S.erase x) 0 x false = CatchUpOutcome.win.
declarations.statement:
theorem catch_up_value_eq_loss_iff (S : Finset ℕ) (hS : S.Nonempty) :
    catch_up_value S = CatchUpOutcome.loss ↔
      ∀ x ∈ S, catch_up_value_aux (S.erase x) 0 x false = CatchUpOutcome.win
declarations.source:
/-- Characterization of loss in Catch-Up: Player 1 loses if and only if Player 2 wins after every opening move. -/
theorem catch_up_value_eq_loss_iff (S : Finset ℕ) (hS : S.Nonempty) :
    catch_up_value S = CatchUpOutcome.loss ↔
      ∀ x ∈ S, catch_up_value_aux (S.erase x) 0 x false = CatchUpOutcome.win := by
  rw [catch_up_value_eq_aux_false, catch_up_value_aux_zero_zero S hS,
    catch_up_outcome_best_eq_loss]
  simp [catch_up_outcome_neg_eq_loss_iff]
declarations.citation: Catch-Up: A Game in Which the Lead Alternates (2015)
declarations.reading: For any finite set of natural numbers $S$, assuming $S$ is non-empty, the catch-up game value `catch_up_value S` is equal to `CatchUpOutcome.loss` if and only if for every element $x \in S$, the auxiliary game value `catch_up_value_aux (S.erase x) 0 x false` is equal to `CatchUpOutcome.win`.

explanation.summary: In Catch-Up on a nonempty set S, Player 1 loses if and only if Player 2 wins after every possible opening move x ∈ S. The proof expands the overall game value into the best outcome among all opening moves, where each move's value is the negation of Player 2's subsequent outcome. Because the best outcome is a loss exactly when all available choices result in a loss, and an outcome is a loss if and only if its negation is a win, Player 1 loses precisely when Player 2 wins against every opening move.

steps.claim: The overall game value being a loss is equivalent to every opening move resulting in a loss for the first player.
steps.explanation: Rewriting with `catch_up_value_eq_aux_false` expresses `catch_up_value S` via the auxiliary evaluation `catch_up_value_aux S 0 0 false`. Since S is nonempty, `catch_up_value_aux_zero_zero` expands this into the best outcome (`CatchUpOutcome.best`) among all candidate opening moves x ∈ S, where each move gives the negated outcome of the second player's resulting position. Then `catch_up_outcome_best_eq_loss` rewrites the condition that the best outcome is a loss into the requirement that every move's outcome is a loss.
steps.code:
rw [catch_up_value_eq_aux_false, catch_up_value_aux_zero_zero S hS,
    catch_up_outcome_best_eq_loss]

steps.claim: Player 1 loses if and only if Player 2 wins after every opening move x ∈ S.
steps.explanation: Simplifying across the list of elements of S transforms membership in S.attach.toList into universal quantification over x ∈ S. Rewriting with `catch_up_outcome_neg_eq_loss_iff` then turns the condition that each move's negated outcome is a loss into the condition that the outcome itself is a win. This makes both sides of the `↔` identical and closes the goal.
steps.code: simp [catch_up_outcome_neg_eq_loss_iff]

glossary.catch_up_value_eq_aux_false: The Catch-Up game value of a set S equals the auxiliary evaluation starting from scores 0 and 0 with the initial-move flag set to false.
glossary.catch_up_value_aux_zero_zero: For a nonempty set S starting at scores 0 and 0, the auxiliary game value is the best outcome among all opening moves x ∈ S, where each move yields the negation of the opponent's outcome from the remaining set S \\ {x} with scores 0 and x.
glossary.catch_up_outcome_best_eq_loss: The best outcome in a list of outcomes is a loss if and only if every outcome in the list is a loss.
glossary.catch_up_outcome_neg_eq_loss_iff: The negation of an outcome is a loss if and only if that outcome is a win.

declarations.name: catch_up_value_aux_empty_eq_draw_iff
declarations.informal: In a Catch-Up position with an empty set of remaining pieces, the game value for the mover is CatchUpOutcome.draw if and only if the mover's score equals the opponent's score.
declarations.statement:
theorem catch_up_value_aux_empty_eq_draw_iff (s_me s_opp : ℕ) (isFirstMove : Bool) :
    catch_up_value_aux ∅ s_me s_opp isFirstMove = CatchUpOutcome.draw ↔ s_me = s_opp
declarations.source:
/-- When no pieces remain in Catch-Up, the position is a draw if and only if the player scores are equal. -/
theorem catch_up_value_aux_empty_eq_draw_iff (s_me s_opp : ℕ) (isFirstMove : Bool) :
    catch_up_value_aux ∅ s_me s_opp isFirstMove = CatchUpOutcome.draw ↔ s_me = s_opp := by
  rw [catch_up_value_aux_empty]
  split_ifs <;> simp <;> omega
declarations.citation: Catch-Up: A Game in Which the Lead Alternates (2015)
declarations.reading: For all natural numbers `s_me` and `s_opp`, and for any boolean `isFirstMove`, `catch_up_value_aux ∅ s_me s_opp isFirstMove` evaluates to `CatchUpOutcome.draw` if and only if `s_me = s_opp`.

explanation.summary: The proof unfolds the terminal evaluation of the game on an empty set of pieces into a three-way case distinction: a win if the mover leads, a loss if the opponent leads, and a draw otherwise. Splitting on these score inequalities and simplifying reduces each branch to an elementary linear arithmetic fact, verified by omega.

steps.claim: Evaluating catch_up_value_aux on an empty set reduces to checking whether the score-comparison conditional equals draw.
steps.explanation: We rewrite using catch_up_value_aux_empty, which expresses the terminal value of the game as a nested if-then-else: win if s_me > s_opp, loss if s_opp > s_me, and draw otherwise.
steps.code: rw [catch_up_value_aux_empty]

steps.claim: The condition evaluates to draw if and only if s_me = s_opp.
steps.explanation: Splitting on the if-then-else conditions yields three cases: if s_me > s_opp, the position is a win (not a draw) and the scores are unequal, so both sides of the equivalence are false; if s_opp > s_me, the position is a loss and the scores are unequal, so again both sides are false; and if neither inequality holds, the position is a draw and trichotomy of natural numbers implies s_me = s_opp, so both sides are true. Simplification and linear arithmetic (omega) close each branch.
steps.code: split_ifs <;> simp <;> omega

glossary.catch_up_value_aux_empty: When the remaining pieces set is empty, the game outcome is a win if s_me > s_opp, a loss if s_opp > s_me, and a draw otherwise.

declarations.name: graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card
declarations.informal: In any finite simple graph G on vertex set V, twice the matching number is at most the number of vertices, 2 * graph_matching_num G ≤ |V|.
declarations.statement:
theorem graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    2 * graph_matching_num G ≤ (Fintype.card V : ℕ∞)
declarations.source:
lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoints_of_mem_edgeSet {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) (e : M.edgeSet) :
    ∃ p : V × V, e.1 = s(p.1, p.2) ∧ M.Adj p.1 p.2 := by
  obtain ⟨e_val, he⟩ := e
  induction e_val using Sym2.ind with
  | h u v =>
    exact ⟨(u, v), rfl, he⟩

noncomputable def graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) (e : M.edgeSet) : V × V :=
  Classical.choose (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoints_of_mem_edgeSet M e)

lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) (e : M.edgeSet) :
    e.1 = s((graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M e).1, (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M e).2) ∧
    M.Adj (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M e).1 (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M e).2 :=
  Classical.choose_spec (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoints_of_mem_edgeSet M e)

lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint1 {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMatching) (e : M.edgeSet) :
    hM.toEdge ⟨(graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M e).1,
      (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).2.fst_mem⟩ = e := by
  have := hM.toEdge_eq_of_adj (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).2
  apply Subtype.ext
  have h_val := congr_arg Subtype.val this
  exact h_val.trans (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).1.symm

lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint2 {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMatching) (e : M.edgeSet) :
    hM.toEdge ⟨(graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M e).2,
      (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).2.snd_mem⟩ = e := by
  have := hM.toEdge_eq_of_adj (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).2.symm
  apply Subtype.ext
  have h_val := congr_arg Subtype.val this
  exact h_val.trans (Sym2.eq_swap.trans (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).1.symm)

noncomputable def graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) (p : Fin 2 × M.edgeSet) : V :=
  if p.1 = 0 then (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p.2).1
  else (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p.2).2

lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_mem_verts {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    (M : G.Subgraph) (p : Fin 2 × M.edgeSet) :
    graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p ∈ M.verts := by
  dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
  split_ifs
  · exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p.2).2.fst_mem
  · exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p.2).2.snd_mem

lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMatching) (p : Fin 2 × M.edgeSet) :
    hM.toEdge ⟨graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p,
      graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_mem_verts M p⟩ = p.2 := by
  dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
  split_ifs
  · exact graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint1 hM p.2
  · exact graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint2 hM p.2

lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_fin2_ne_cases {i j : Fin 2} (h : i ≠ j) :
    (i = 0 ∧ j = 1) ∨ (i = 1 ∧ j = 0) := by
  revert i j
  decide

lemma graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_injective {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V}
    {M : G.Subgraph} (hM : M.IsMatching) :
    Function.Injective (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M) := by
  intro p₁ p₂ h
  have he : p₁.2 = p₂.2 := by
    have h1 := graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint hM p₁
    have h2 := graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint hM p₂
    have h_eq : (⟨graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₁,
                   graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_mem_verts M p₁⟩ : M.verts) =
                ⟨graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₂,
                 graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_mem_verts M p₂⟩ := Subtype.ext h
    rw [h_eq] at h1
    exact h1.symm.trans h2
  have hi : p₁.1 = p₂.1 := by
    by_contra hne
    rcases graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_fin2_ne_cases hne with ⟨h0, h1⟩ | ⟨h1, h0⟩
    · exfalso
      have hp1 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₁ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₁.2).1 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_pos h0]
      have hp2 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₂ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₂.2).2 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_neg (by rw [h1]; decide)]
      rw [hp1, hp2, he] at h
      exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p₂.2).2.ne h
    · exfalso
      have hp1 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₁ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₁.2).2 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_neg (by rw [h1]; decide)]
      have hp2 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₂ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₂.2).1 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_pos h0]
      rw [hp1, hp2, he] at h
      exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p₂.2).2.symm.ne h
  exact Prod.ext hi he

/-- Twice the matching number is at most the number of vertices in a finite graph. -/
theorem graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    2 * graph_matching_num G ≤ (Fintype.card V : ℕ∞) := by
  dsimp [graph_matching_num]
  rw [ENat.mul_iSup]
  refine iSup_le fun M ↦ ?_
  rw [ENat.mul_iSup]
  refine iSup_le fun hM ↦ ?_
  have hinj := graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_injective hM
  have hcard := ENat.card_le_card_of_injective hinj
  have hprod : ENat.card (Fin 2 × M.edgeSet) = 2 * M.edgeSet.encard := by
    rw [ENat.card_prod, ENat.card_coe_set_eq]
    simp
  rw [ENat.card_eq_coe_fintype_card (α := V)] at hcard
  exact hprod ▸ hcard
declarations.reading: For every finite type `V` and every simple graph `G` on `V`, twice the matching number of `G` (`graph_matching_num G`) is less than or equal to the cardinality of `V` (coerced to `ℕ∞`).

explanation.summary: The theorem states that in any finite graph G, twice the matching number is at most the total number of vertices: 2 * ν(G) ≤ |V|. The argument shows that for any matching M, there is an injective map from Fin 2 × M.edgeSet to V sending each edge to its two endpoints. Because each vertex in a matching belongs to at most one matching edge and the two endpoints of an edge are distinct, this map is injective, giving 2 * |M.edgeSet| ≤ |V|; taking the supremum over all matchings M completes the proof.

steps.claim: Every edge in a subgraph M can be written as an unordered pair s(u, v) whose endpoints u and v are adjacent in M.
steps.explanation: Unpacking the edge subtype e and applying induction on Sym2 via `Sym2.ind`, any edge is represented as s(u, v). Its adjacency in M follows directly from the membership hypothesis of the edge in M.edgeSet.
steps.code:
obtain ⟨e_val, he⟩ := e
  induction e_val using Sym2.ind with
  | h u v =>
    exact ⟨(u, v), rfl, he⟩

steps.claim: For any edge e in a matching M, applying the matching map `toEdge` to its first endpoint recovers e.
steps.explanation: By `toEdge_eq_of_adj`, any matched vertex adjacent to another vertex in M has that edge as its unique incident edge in M. Passing to the underlying values and using `Subtype.ext` shows this matches e.
steps.code:
have := hM.toEdge_eq_of_adj (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).2
  apply Subtype.ext
  have h_val := congr_arg Subtype.val this
  exact h_val.trans (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).1.symm

steps.claim: For any edge e in a matching M, applying `toEdge` to its second endpoint recovers e.
steps.explanation: By symmetry of adjacency, the second endpoint is adjacent to the first in M. Applying `toEdge` gives the edge s(v, u), which equals s(u, v) = e by `Sym2.eq_swap`.
steps.code:
have := hM.toEdge_eq_of_adj (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).2.symm
  apply Subtype.ext
  have h_val := congr_arg Subtype.val this
  exact h_val.trans (Sym2.eq_swap.trans (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M e).1.symm)

steps.claim: For every indexed edge in `Fin 2 × M.edgeSet`, the selected endpoint belongs to M.verts.
steps.explanation: Unfolding the definition of `endpoint`, the vertex is either the first or second endpoint of the edge. Since the two endpoints are adjacent in M, both belong to M.verts.
steps.code:
dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
  split_ifs
  · exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p.2).2.fst_mem
  · exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p.2).2.snd_mem

steps.claim: Applying `toEdge` to the i-th endpoint of an edge e recovers e for any index i.
steps.explanation: Case-splitting on whether i = 0 or i = 1 reduces directly to `toEdge_endpoint1` and `toEdge_endpoint2` respectively.
steps.code:
dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
  split_ifs
  · exact graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint1 hM p.2
  · exact graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint2 hM p.2

steps.claim: Any two distinct elements of Fin 2 are either 0 and 1, or 1 and 0.
steps.explanation: There are only two elements in Fin 2, so exhaustively checking the finite possibilities confirms that unequal elements must be 0 and 1 in some order.
steps.code:
revert i j
  decide

steps.claim: If two indexed edges map to the same vertex, they must share the same edge component.
steps.explanation: If f(p₁) = f(p₂) as vertices, applying `toEdge` to both sides yields p₁.2 = toEdge(f(p₁)) = toEdge(f(p₂)) = p₂.2, because a matched vertex belongs to a unique edge in the matching.
steps.code:
intro p₁ p₂ h
  have he : p₁.2 = p₂.2 := by
    have h1 := graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint hM p₁
    have h2 := graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdge_endpoint hM p₂
    have h_eq : (⟨graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₁,
                   graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_mem_verts M p₁⟩ : M.verts) =
                ⟨graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₂,
                 graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_mem_verts M p₂⟩ := Subtype.ext h
    rw [h_eq] at h1
    exact h1.symm.trans h2

steps.claim: If two indexed edges map to the same vertex, their index components also match, proving the endpoint map is injective.
steps.explanation: If p₁.1 ≠ p₂.1, then one index is 0 and the other is 1. Since p₁.2 = p₂.2, this would mean the two endpoints of that same edge are equal to each other. But adjacent vertices in a simple graph are always distinct, giving a contradiction. Hence p₁.1 = p₂.1, and `Prod.ext` gives p₁ = p₂.
steps.code:
have hi : p₁.1 = p₂.1 := by
    by_contra hne
    rcases graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_fin2_ne_cases hne with ⟨h0, h1⟩ | ⟨h1, h0⟩
    · exfalso
      have hp1 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₁ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₁.2).1 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_pos h0]
      have hp2 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₂ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₂.2).2 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_neg (by rw [h1]; decide)]
      rw [hp1, hp2, he] at h
      exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p₂.2).2.ne h
    · exfalso
      have hp1 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₁ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₁.2).2 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_neg (by rw [h1]; decide)]
      have hp2 : graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint M p₂ =
          (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints M p₂.2).1 := by
        dsimp [graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint]
        rw [if_pos h0]
      rw [hp1, hp2, he] at h
      exact (graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeEndpoints_spec M p₂.2).2.symm.ne h
  exact Prod.ext hi he

steps.claim: Bounding 2 * graph_matching_num G ≤ |V| reduces to showing 2 * |M.edgeSet| ≤ |V| for every matching M.
steps.explanation: The matching number is defined as the supremum of |M.edgeSet| over all matchings M. Distributing multiplication by 2 over the supremum via `ENat.mul_iSup` and using `iSup_le`, it suffices to bound each matching individually.
steps.code:
dsimp [graph_matching_num]
  rw [ENat.mul_iSup]
  refine iSup_le fun M ↦ ?_
  rw [ENat.mul_iSup]
  refine iSup_le fun hM ↦ ?_

steps.claim: For every matching M, 2 * |M.edgeSet| ≤ |V|, concluding the theorem.
steps.explanation: Because the endpoint map `Fin 2 × M.edgeSet → V` is injective, the cardinality of `Fin 2 × M.edgeSet` is at most |V|. Since |Fin 2 × M.edgeSet| = 2 * |M.edgeSet|, this establishes 2 * |M.edgeSet| ≤ |V|.
steps.code:
have hinj := graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpoint_injective hM
  have hcard := ENat.card_le_card_of_injective hinj
  have hprod : ENat.card (Fin 2 × M.edgeSet) = 2 * M.edgeSet.encard := by
    rw [ENat.card_prod, ENat.card_coe_set_eq]
    simp
  rw [ENat.card_eq_coe_fintype_card (α := V)] at hcard
  exact hprod ▸ hcard

glossary.Sym2.ind: To prove a statement for all unordered pairs in `Sym2 α`, it suffices to prove it for pairs of the form `s(x, y)`.
glossary.graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_edgeE: The chosen pair of vertices for an edge `e` in a subgraph `M` satisfies `e = s(u, v)` and `u` is adjacent to `v` in `M`.
glossary.Subtype.ext: Two terms of a subtype are equal if and only if their underlying values are equal.
glossary.congr_arg: Equality is preserved under function application: if `a = b` then `f a = f b`.
glossary.Subtype.val: Extracts the underlying value of a subtype term.
glossary.Sym2.eq_swap: The unordered pair `s(a, b)` is identical to `s(b, a)`.
glossary.graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpo: Maps an indexed edge `(i, e) ∈ Fin 2 × M.edgeSet` to the first endpoint of `e` if `i = 0`, and the second endpoint otherwise.
glossary.graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_toEdg: Applying the matching map `toEdge` to the first chosen endpoint of an edge `e` returns `e`.
Applying the matching map `toEdge` to the second chosen endpoint of an edge `e` returns `e`.
Applying the matching map `toEdge` to either endpoint of an edge `e` returns `e`.
glossary.graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpo: The endpoint chosen for any indexed edge in `Fin 2 × M.edgeSet` is a vertex of `M`.
glossary.graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_fin2_: Two distinct elements of `Fin 2` must be 0 and 1 in one order or the other.
glossary.if_pos: An `if-then-else` expression reduces to the `then` branch when the condition is true.
glossary.if_neg: An `if-then-else` expression reduces to the `else` branch when the condition is false.
glossary.Prod.ext: Two ordered pairs are equal if their first components are equal and their second components are equal.
glossary.ENat.mul_iSup: Multiplication by a scalar distributes over an arbitrary supremum in `ℕ∞`.
glossary.iSup_le: A supremum is at most `a` if and only if every element in the family is at most `a`.
glossary.graph_matching_num_two_mul_le_card_endpo: The endpoint assignment map from `Fin 2 × M.edgeSet` to `V` is injective for any matching `M`.
glossary.ENat.card_le_card_of_injective: An injection from `α` to `β` implies `ENat.card α ≤ ENat.card β`.
glossary.ENat.card_prod: The cardinality of a product type is the product of the cardinalities of its factor types.
glossary.ENat.card_coe_set_eq: The cardinality of the subtype coerced from a set `s` equals `s.encard`.
glossary.ENat.card_eq_coe_fintype_card: For a finite type, `ENat.card` equals the coerced `Fintype.card`.

The matching number is defined in `ℕ∞` as a supremum, so the cardinal arithmetic is performed over extended natural numbers using lemmas such as `ENat.mul_iSup` and `ENat.card_prod`.

declarations.name: tarski_query_complexity_one_le_log
declarations.informal: One-dimensional Tarski by binary search: for n ≥ 1, a fixed point of any monotone map on the chain {0, …, n−1} can be found with at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 queries.
declarations.statement:
theorem tarski_query_complexity_one_le_log (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    tarski_query_complexity_le n 1 (Nat.log 2 n + 1)
declarations.source:
/-- The point `min i m` of the chain `{0, …, m}`, as a point of `[m+1]^1`. -/
def tarski_one_pt (m i : ℕ) : Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1) := fun _ => ⟨min i m, by omega⟩

/-- Binary search on `[lo, hi]` with `d` levels of fuel. -/
def tarski_one_bs (m : ℕ) : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ → TarskiQueryTree (m + 1) 1
  | 0, lo, _ => .output (tarski_one_pt m lo)
  | d + 1, lo, hi =>
    .query (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) (fun y =>
      if (y 0 : ℕ) = (lo + hi) / 2 then .output (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2))
      else if (y 0 : ℕ) < (lo + hi) / 2 then tarski_one_bs m d lo ((lo + hi) / 2 - 1)
      else tarski_one_bs m d ((lo + hi) / 2 + 1) hi)

theorem tarski_one_pt_val (m i : ℕ) (j : Fin 1) : ((tarski_one_pt m i j : Fin (m + 1)) : ℕ) = min i m :=
  rfl

theorem tarski_one_pt_mono (m : ℕ) {i j : ℕ} (h : i ≤ j) : tarski_one_pt m i ≤ tarski_one_pt m j := by
  intro x
  show ((tarski_one_pt m i x : Fin (m + 1)) : ℕ) ≤ tarski_one_pt m j x
  simp only [tarski_one_pt_val]
  omega

theorem tarski_one_eq_pt (m i : ℕ) (hi : i ≤ m) (x : Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1)) (h : (x 0 : ℕ) = i) :
    x = tarski_one_pt m i := by
  funext j
  have : j = 0 := Subsingleton.elim _ _
  subst this
  apply Fin.ext
  rw [h, tarski_one_pt_val]
  omega

theorem tarski_one_bs_spec (m : ℕ) (f : (Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1)) → (Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1)))
    (hf : Monotone f) :
    ∀ d lo hi, lo ≤ hi → hi ≤ m → hi - lo + 1 < 2 ^ (d + 1) →
      lo ≤ (f (tarski_one_pt m lo) 0 : ℕ) → (f (tarski_one_pt m hi) 0 : ℕ) ≤ hi →
      f ((tarski_one_bs m d lo hi).run f) = (tarski_one_bs m d lo hi).run f ∧
        (tarski_one_bs m d lo hi).cost f ≤ d + 1 := by
  have hmono : ∀ {i j : ℕ}, i ≤ j →
      (f (tarski_one_pt m i) 0 : ℕ) ≤ f (tarski_one_pt m j) 0 :=
    fun h => hf (tarski_one_pt_mono m h) 0
  intro d
  induction d with
  | zero =>
    intro lo hi hlh hhm hsz hlo hhi
    have : hi = lo := by simp at hsz; omega
    subst this
    refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
    · simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run]
      exact tarski_one_eq_pt m hi hhm _ (by omega)
    · simp [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.cost]
  | succ d ih =>
    intro lo hi hlh hhm hsz hlo hhi
    have hP : 2 ^ (d + 1 + 1) = 2 * 2 ^ (d + 1) := by ring
    by_cases h1 : (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) = (lo + hi) / 2
    · simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run, TarskiQueryTree.cost, h1, if_true]
      exact ⟨tarski_one_eq_pt m _ (by omega) _ h1, by omega⟩
    by_cases h2 : (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) < (lo + hi) / 2
    · have hl : lo ≤ (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) :=
        le_trans hlo (hmono (by omega))
      have := ih lo ((lo + hi) / 2 - 1) (by omega) (by omega) (by omega) hlo
        (by have := hmono (show (lo + hi) / 2 - 1 ≤ (lo + hi) / 2 by omega); omega)
      simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run, TarskiQueryTree.cost, h1, h2, if_false,
        if_true]
      exact ⟨this.1, by omega⟩
    · have hh : (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) ≤ hi := le_trans (hmono (by omega)) hhi
      have := ih ((lo + hi) / 2 + 1) hi (by omega) hhm (by omega)
        (by have := hmono (show (lo + hi) / 2 ≤ (lo + hi) / 2 + 1 by omega); omega) hhi
      simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run, TarskiQueryTree.cost, h1, h2, if_false]
      exact ⟨this.1, by omega⟩

theorem tarski_query_complexity_one_le_log (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    tarski_query_complexity_le n 1 (Nat.log 2 n + 1) := by
  obtain ⟨m, rfl⟩ : ∃ m, n = m + 1 := ⟨n - 1, by omega⟩
  refine ⟨tarski_one_bs m (Nat.log 2 (m + 1)) 0 m, fun f hf => ?_⟩
  have hlt := Nat.lt_pow_succ_log_self (b := 2) (by norm_num) (m + 1)
  exact tarski_one_bs_spec m f hf _ 0 m (Nat.zero_le _) le_rfl (by omega) (Nat.zero_le _)
    (by have := (f (tarski_one_pt m m) 0).isLt; omega)
declarations.citation: arXiv:2610.07055 (Tarski fixed points in quasi-FPT queries), Sec. 1 (the binary search baseline, which the recursive algorithm giving O(log^k n) builds on); the case k = 1

explanation.summary: The one-dimensional Tarski fixed point theorem on {0, …, n−1} is proved by binary search. Given a monotone function f and an interval [lo, hi] with f(lo) ≥ lo and f(hi) ≤ hi, querying the midpoint either finds a fixed point immediately or preserves the boundary invariants on a subinterval of half the size. Initializing on [0, n−1] with fuel depth ⌊log₂ n⌋ ensures the search terminates at a fixed point within ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 queries.

steps.claim: The function tarski_one_pt embeds an index i into the chain Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1) as min(i, m).
steps.explanation: The point assigns to the single coordinate in Fin 1 the value min(i, m). Linear arithmetic verifies that min(i, m) < m + 1 so that it is a valid element of Fin (m + 1).
steps.code:
/-- The point `min i m` of the chain `{0, …, m}`, as a point of `[m+1]^1`. -/
def tarski_one_pt (m i : ℕ) : Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1) := fun _ => ⟨min i m, by omega⟩

steps.claim: The embedding tarski_one_pt is monotone in the index.
steps.explanation: Given i ≤ j, we compare tarski_one_pt m i and tarski_one_pt m j pointwise at their single coordinate. Rewriting with tarski_one_pt_val reduces this to min(i, m) ≤ min(j, m), which holds by linear arithmetic.
steps.code:
theorem tarski_one_pt_mono (m : ℕ) {i j : ℕ} (h : i ≤ j) : tarski_one_pt m i ≤ tarski_one_pt m j := by
  intro x
  show ((tarski_one_pt m i x : Fin (m + 1)) : ℕ) ≤ tarski_one_pt m j x
  simp only [tarski_one_pt_val]
  omega

steps.claim: Any point x in Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1) whose single coordinate is i ≤ m equals tarski_one_pt m i.
steps.explanation: By function extensionality, it suffices to check the single coordinate j : Fin 1. Since Fin 1 is a subsingleton, Subsingleton.elim gives j = 0. By Fin.ext, the equality reduces to x(0) = min(i, m), which holds by tarski_one_pt_val and the assumption i ≤ m.
steps.code:
theorem tarski_one_eq_pt (m i : ℕ) (hi : i ≤ m) (x : Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1)) (h : (x 0 : ℕ) = i) :
    x = tarski_one_pt m i := by
  funext j
  have : j = 0 := Subsingleton.elim _ _
  subst this
  apply Fin.ext
  rw [h, tarski_one_pt_val]
  omega

steps.claim: Monotone maps preserve chain order, and the binary search specification tarski_one_bs_spec holds in the base case d = 0.
steps.explanation: Composing f with the monotone embedding tarski_one_pt_mono shows that f is monotone in the index. We proceed by induction on depth d. When d = 0, the length condition (hi - lo + 1) < 2 forces hi = lo. The boundary conditions lo ≤ f(lo)₀ and f(hi)₀ ≤ hi then sandwich f(lo)₀ = lo. By tarski_one_eq_pt, this point is a fixed point of f, and the query tree outputs it with cost 0 ≤ 0 + 1.
steps.code:
theorem tarski_one_bs_spec (m : ℕ) (f : (Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1)) → (Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1)))
    (hf : Monotone f) :
    ∀ d lo hi, lo ≤ hi → hi ≤ m → hi - lo + 1 < 2 ^ (d + 1) →
      lo ≤ (f (tarski_one_pt m lo) 0 : ℕ) → (f (tarski_one_pt m hi) 0 : ℕ) ≤ hi →
      f ((tarski_one_bs m d lo hi).run f) = (tarski_one_bs m d lo hi).run f ∧
        (tarski_one_bs m d lo hi).cost f ≤ d + 1 := by
  have hmono : ∀ {i j : ℕ}, i ≤ j →
      (f (tarski_one_pt m i) 0 : ℕ) ≤ f (tarski_one_pt m j) 0 :=
    fun h => hf (tarski_one_pt_mono m h) 0
  intro d
  induction d with
  | zero =>
    intro lo hi hlh hhm hsz hlo hhi
    have : hi = lo := by simp at hsz; omega
    subst this
    refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
    · simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run]
      exact tarski_one_eq_pt m hi hhm _ (by omega)
    · simp [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.cost]

steps.claim: In the inductive step, if the midpoint is already a fixed point, the search tree outputs it immediately.
steps.explanation: We query the midpoint mid = (lo + hi) / 2. If f(mid)₀ = mid, then tarski_one_eq_pt identifies mid as a fixed point of f. The tree outputs it using 1 query, which is at most (d + 1) + 1.
steps.code:
| succ d ih =>
    intro lo hi hlh hhm hsz hlo hhi
    have hP : 2 ^ (d + 1 + 1) = 2 * 2 ^ (d + 1) := by ring
    by_cases h1 : (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) = (lo + hi) / 2
    · simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run, TarskiQueryTree.cost, h1, if_true]
      exact ⟨tarski_one_eq_pt m _ (by omega) _ h1, by omega⟩

steps.claim: If f(mid)₀ < mid, the search recurses on the lower subinterval [lo, mid - 1].
steps.explanation: When f(mid)₀ < mid, the boundary conditions lo ≤ f(lo)₀ and f(mid - 1)₀ ≤ mid - 1 are preserved by transitivity (le_trans) and monotonicity of f. The new subinterval has length strictly less than 2^(d + 1). Applying the induction hypothesis gives a fixed point with query cost at most d + 1, so the total cost including the midpoint query is at most d + 2.
steps.code:
by_cases h2 : (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) < (lo + hi) / 2
    · have hl : lo ≤ (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) :=
        le_trans hlo (hmono (by omega))
      have := ih lo ((lo + hi) / 2 - 1) (by omega) (by omega) (by omega) hlo
        (by have := hmono (show (lo + hi) / 2 - 1 ≤ (lo + hi) / 2 by omega); omega)
      simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run, TarskiQueryTree.cost, h1, h2, if_false,
        if_true]
      exact ⟨this.1, by omega⟩

steps.claim: If f(mid)₀ > mid, the search recurses on the upper subinterval [mid + 1, hi].
steps.explanation: When f(mid)₀ > mid, the boundary conditions mid + 1 ≤ f(mid + 1)₀ and f(hi)₀ ≤ hi are preserved by transitivity (le_trans) and monotonicity. The new subinterval length is strictly less than 2^(d + 1). Applying the induction hypothesis yields a fixed point with total query cost at most d + 2.
steps.code:
· have hh : (f (tarski_one_pt m ((lo + hi) / 2)) 0 : ℕ) ≤ hi := le_trans (hmono (by omega)) hhi
      have := ih ((lo + hi) / 2 + 1) hi (by omega) hhm (by omega)
        (by have := hmono (show (lo + hi) / 2 ≤ (lo + hi) / 2 + 1 by omega); omega) hhi
      simp only [tarski_one_bs, TarskiQueryTree.run, TarskiQueryTree.cost, h1, h2, if_false]
      exact ⟨this.1, by omega⟩

steps.claim: For the main theorem, rewrite n as m + 1 and instantiate the binary search tree on [0, m].
steps.explanation: Since n ≥ 1, we write n = m + 1 for m = n - 1. We choose the binary search tree tarski_one_bs with fuel depth ⌊log₂ (m + 1)⌋ on the initial interval [0, m].
steps.code:
theorem tarski_query_complexity_one_le_log (n : ℕ) (hn : 1 ≤ n) :
    tarski_query_complexity_le n 1 (Nat.log 2 n + 1) := by
  obtain ⟨m, rfl⟩ : ∃ m, n = m + 1 := ⟨n - 1, by omega⟩
  refine ⟨tarski_one_bs m (Nat.log 2 (m + 1)) 0 m, fun f hf => ?_⟩

steps.claim: The binary search tree finds a fixed point of f within ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 queries.
steps.explanation: We apply tarski_one_bs_spec on [0, m]. The interval size m + 1 is strictly less than 2^(⌊log₂ (m + 1)⌋ + 1) by Nat.lt_pow_succ_log_self. The lower boundary condition 0 ≤ f(0)₀ holds by Nat.zero_le, and the upper boundary condition f(m)₀ ≤ m holds because the codomain is Fin (m + 1) by Fin.isLt. Reflexivity le_rfl handles m ≤ m.
steps.code:
have hlt := Nat.lt_pow_succ_log_self (b := 2) (by norm_num) (m + 1)
  exact tarski_one_bs_spec m f hf _ 0 m (Nat.zero_le _) le_rfl (by omega) (Nat.zero_le _)
    (by have := (f (tarski_one_pt m m) 0).isLt; omega)

glossary.Fin.ext: Two elements of `Fin n` are equal if and only if their underlying natural values are equal.
glossary.Fin.isLt: The underlying natural value of any element of `Fin n` is strictly less than n.
glossary.le_rfl: Reflexivity of less-than-or-equal: every element in a preorder is ≤ itself.
glossary.le_trans: Transitivity of less-than-or-equal: if a ≤ b and b ≤ c, then a ≤ c.
glossary.Nat.lt_pow_succ_log_self: For any base b > 1 and natural number x, x is strictly less than b^(⌊log_b x⌋ + 1).
glossary.Nat.zero_le: Zero is less than or equal to any natural number.
glossary.Subsingleton.elim: Any two elements of a subsingleton type are equal. In particular, any index j : Fin 1 is equal to 0.
glossary.tarski_one_bs_spec: Given a monotone map f on the chain {0, …, m} and an interval [lo, hi] satisfying the boundary conditions lo ≤ f(lo)₀ and f(hi)₀ ≤ hi with length strictly less than 2^(d + 1), binary search of depth d returns a fixed point of f using at most d + 1 queries.
glossary.tarski_one_eq_pt: For i ≤ m, any point x in Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1) with x(0) = i is equal to tarski_one_pt m i.
glossary.tarski_one_pt_mono: Embedding indices into the 1-dimensional chain is monotone: if i ≤ j, then tarski_one_pt m i ≤ tarski_one_pt m j.
glossary.tarski_one_pt_val: The value of the single coordinate of tarski_one_pt m i is min(i, m).

caveats: The 1-dimensional chain of size n = m + 1 is formalized as functions `Fin 1 → Fin (m + 1)`, representing points on a grid with dimension 1. Consequently, points have a single coordinate at index 0.
