literature.rationale: The smallest case where exact MMS can fail. The $11/12$ guarantee (arXiv:2205.05363) is shown best possible for a restricted kind of allocation (one prespecified agent gets her full proportional share), so improving it needs new ideas. The $39/40$ example (three agents, nine goods; arXiv:2104.04977) is proven to be the worst possible among instances with fewer than six more items than agents, so any better impossibility needs at least ten goods. With three agents the problem is small enough for computer-assisted search on the impossibility side.

literature.title: Polynomial-time computation of EF1 and Pareto-optimal allocations of goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. An allocation is an ordered partition $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$ (every good is allocated; bundles may be empty). Values are given as nonnegative integers (or rationals) in binary. An allocation is EF1 if for all $i\ne j$ with $A_j\ne\emptyset$ there is $g\in A_j$ with $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$, and Pareto optimal (PO) if no allocation $B$ has $v_i(B_i)\ge v_i(A_i)$ for all $i$ with strict inequality for some $i$. An EF1+PO allocation always exists (e.g. a maximum Nash welfare allocation). Question: is there an algorithm that outputs an EF1+PO allocation in time polynomial in $n$, $m$ and the bit length of the values?
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.rationale: Existence follows from maximum Nash welfare ('The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare'), but computing that allocation is APX-hard. A market-based pseudo-polynomial algorithm finds EF1+PO (arXiv:1707.04731); polynomial time is known for a fixed number of agents (arXiv:2411.01810), for binary and other few-valued instances, and for EF1+fPO under extra structure. For chores, EF1+PO existence was settled in 2025 (arXiv:2507.09544), but only with polynomial time for constant $n$. A general polynomial algorithm, or evidence of hardness (e.g. PLS/PPAD), is open.

literature.title: EF1 and Pareto optimality for mixed goods and chores
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents and a finite set $M$ of indivisible items. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{o\in S}v_i(o)$ with $v_i(o)\in\mathbb{R}$ of arbitrary sign (an item may be a good for one agent and a chore for another). An allocation is a partition $(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$. It is EF1 if for all $i\ne j$, either $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j)$ or there is an item $o\in A_i\cup A_j$ with $v_i(A_i\setminus\{o\})\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{o\})$. It is Pareto optimal if no allocation $B$ has $v_i(B_i)\ge v_i(A_i)$ for all $i$ with strict inequality for some $i$. Question: does every such instance (for every $n\ge 3$) admit an allocation that is both EF1 and Pareto optimal?
literature.source_title: Fair allocation of combinations of indivisible goods and chores
literature.rationale: For goods, maximum Nash welfare gives EF1+PO; for chores, existence was proven only in 2025 by a fixed-point argument (arXiv:2507.09544). For mixed manna, EF1 alone is easy (a double round-robin) and EF1+PO is known for two agents (arXiv:1807.10684), but the general case is open, even for three agents. Partial progress: PO with introspective EF1 (arXiv:2509.18673) and PO with envy-freeness up to $n-1$ reallocations (arXiv:2507.03946). A positive answer would unify the goods and chores theories.

literature.title: Query complexity of envy-free cake cutting
literature.statement: The cake is $[0,1]$. Each of $n$ agents has a valuation $v_i$: a nonatomic probability measure on $[0,1]$ (additive, $v_i([0,1])=1$, single points have measure 0). In the Robertson–Webb query model a protocol may ask $\mathrm{Eval}_i(x,y)=v_i([x,y])$ and $\mathrm{Cut}_i(x,\alpha)=$ some $y$ with $v_i([x,y])=\alpha$. It must output an allocation: disjoint pieces $A_1,\dots,A_n$, each a finite union of intervals, covering $[0,1]$, that is envy-free ($v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j)$ for all $i,j$). Let $T(n)$ be the minimum, over protocols, of the worst-case number of queries. Question: is $T(n)$ bounded by a polynomial in $n$? More generally, determine the growth of $T(n)$.
literature.source_title: A Discrete and Bounded Envy-Free Cake Cutting Protocol for Any Number of Agents
literature.rationale: Bounded protocols were found only in 2015-16: four agents (arXiv:1508.05143, improved to about 171 queries in arXiv:1807.00317) and any $n$ with a tower of exponentials (arXiv:1604.03655). A later sharper analysis gave $n^{O(n^2)}$, and a September 2026 preprint claims $n^{O(1)}2^n$ (arXiv:2609.05191; not yet peer-reviewed). The only lower bound is $\Omega(n^2)$ ('Thou Shalt Covet Thy Neighbor's Cake'). Even for $n=4$ the exact query complexity is unknown. With connected pieces, exact envy-freeness cannot be reached by any finite protocol, and the connected approximate version is a separate open question (see OP-18).

literature.title: Best approximation factor for EFX with additive goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. An allocation is an ordered partition $A=(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ of $M$ (every good is allocated; bundles may be empty). For $\alpha\in(0,1]$ an allocation is $\alpha$-EFX if for all $i\ne j$ and all $g\in A_j$, $v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$. Let $\alpha^*$ be the supremum of $\alpha$ such that every instance (any $n$, $m$) admits an $\alpha$-EFX allocation. Currently $\varphi-1=(\sqrt5-1)/2\approx0.618\le\alpha^*\le 1$. Question: determine $\alpha^*$; in particular, does a $2/3$-EFX allocation (or any $\alpha>\varphi-1$) always exist for every $n$?
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.rationale: Envy-cycle elimination gives $1/2$-EFX, and the golden-ratio bound $\varphi-1$ comes from combining round-robin with envy-cycle elimination ('Multiple Birds with One Stone: Beating 1/2 for EFX and GMMS via Envy Cycle Elimination', arXiv:1909.07650). $2/3$-EFX is known for at most seven agents, for valuations with at most three distinct values, and for multigraph instances (arXiv:2406.12413), and $(1-\varepsilon)$-EFX holds if a sublinear number of goods may stay unallocated (arXiv:2205.07638). If OP-7 were refuted, this question would become the main open problem about EFX.

literature.title: EFX together with Pareto optimality for positive additive goods
literature.statement: There are $n\ge 3$ agents and a finite set $M$ of goods; agent $i$ has an additive valuation with strictly positive item values $v_i(g)>0$. An allocation $(A_1,\dots,A_n)$ partitions $M$. It is EFX if $v_i(A_i)\ge v_i(A_j\setminus\{g\})$ for all $i\ne j$ and $g\in A_j$, and Pareto optimal if no allocation $B$ has $v_i(B_i)\ge v_i(A_i)$ for all $i$ with strict inequality for some $i$. Question: does every such instance admit an allocation that is simultaneously EFX and Pareto optimal? (The case $n=3$, where EFX alone is known to exist, is already open.)
literature.source_title: Almost Envy-Freeness with General Valuations
literature.rationale: With zero values EFX and PO can be incompatible even for two agents (arXiv:1707.04769), so strict positivity is the natural assumption; with it, EFX+PO holds for two agents via leximin. Known: bi-valued instances (EFX with fractional PO); two types of goods (arXiv:2601.03438). For chores the analog fails for every $n\ge 4$ even with positive bi-valued costs (arXiv:2606.08872), which raises the question of whether goods behave differently. A counterexample for $n=3$ would be a finite object, which makes this attractive for search plus Lean verification.

literature.title: Exact EFX with a sublinear number of unallocated goods
literature.statement: There are $n$ agents $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a finite set $M$ of $m$ indivisible goods. Agent $i$ has an additive valuation $v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S} v_i(g)$ with $v_i(g)\ge 0$. A partial allocation is a tuple of pairwise disjoint bundles $X_1,\dots,X_n\subseteq M$; the unallocated goods form $P=M\setminus\bigcup_i X_i$. $X$ is EFX if $v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(X_j\setminus\{g\})$ for all $i\ne j$, $g\in X_j$, and no agent envies the pool if $v_i(X_i)\ge v_i(P)$ for all $i$. It is known that some EFX partial allocation with no envy toward the pool always has $|P|\le n-2$ (for $n\ge 2$). Question: is there a function $f(n)=o(n)$ such that every additive instance admits an EFX partial allocation with $|P|\le f(n)$ and no agent envying the pool?
literature.source_title: Fair Division of Indivisible Goods: Recent Progress and Open Questions
literature.rationale: EFX with charity was introduced in arXiv:1902.04319, with the bound of $n-1$ unallocated goods in arXiv:1907.04596, improved to $n-2$ (arXiv:2102.10654; arXiv:2107.09901 for general monotone valuations). Through the rainbow-cycle-number connection, $(1-\varepsilon)$-EFX holds with sublinearly many unallocated goods ($\tilde O((n/\varepsilon)^{1/2})$, arXiv:2205.07638), but for exact EFX nothing sublinear is known. A positive answer to OP-7 would give $f\equiv0$, so this is a weaker stepping stone toward OP-7.

literature.title: Connected approximately envy-free cake cutting for five monotone agents
literature.statement: The cake is $[0,1]$. Each of $n=5$ agents has a valuation $v_i$ assigning a value in $[0,1]$ to every interval $I\subseteq[0,1]$. It is monotone ($I\subseteq J\Rightarrow v_i(I)\le v_i(J)$), Lipschitz-continuous in the endpoints, and accessible only through value queries $v_i([a,b])$. A connected allocation is given by cut points $0\le x_1\le\dots\le x_4\le 1$, which form 5 consecutive intervals, together with a bijection assigning them to agents. It is $\varepsilon$-envy-free if $v_i(I_{\sigma(i)})\ge v_i(I_{\sigma(j)})-\varepsilon$ for all $i,j$. Such allocations always exist. Question: can one be found with $\mathrm{poly}(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ value queries, or is $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ queries necessary?
literature.source_title: Envy-Free Cake-Cutting for Four Agents
literature.rationale: For monotone valuations an efficient algorithm ($\mathrm{poly}(\log 1/\varepsilon)$ queries) was known for three agents ('Algorithmic Solutions for Envy-Free Cake Cutting', Operations Research 2012, which posed four or more agents as open), and arXiv:2311.02075 solved four agents. Without monotonicity the problem becomes PPAD-hard with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ query lower bounds for four agents (arXiv:2311.02075), and in 2026 also for three agents (arXiv:2606.13980). Five monotone agents is the next frontier, and it decides whether monotonicity keeps the problem tractable for every $n$.

literature.title: Condorcet dimension of elections: do 3 candidates always suffice?
literature.statement: Let $N$ be a finite nonempty set of $n$ voters and $C$ a finite set of candidates; each voter $v$ has a strict linear order $\succ_v$ on $C$. A set $S \subseteq C$ is a Condorcet winning set if for every candidate $a \in C \setminus S$, strictly fewer than $n/2$ voters rank $a$ above every member of $S$ (equivalently, a strict majority of voters prefers some member of $S$ to $a$). The Condorcet dimension of the election is the minimum size of a Condorcet winning set. Question: is the Condorcet dimension of every election at most 3? (Weaker open form: at most 4.) It is known that every election has dimension at most 5, and that there exist elections of dimension exactly 3.
literature.source_title: Condorcet winning sets
literature.rationale: The concept was introduced in the paper 'Condorcet winning sets', which exhibited elections needing 3 candidates and conjectured unbounded dimension. 'Six Candidates Suffice to Win a Voter Majority' (arXiv:2411.03390) gave the first constant bound (6) via the minimax theorem and maximal lotteries; 'A few good choices' (arXiv:2506.22133) improved it to 5 (exposition: arXiv:2606.14666). 'Is Four Enough? Automated Reasoning Approaches and Dual Bounds for Condorcet Dimensions of Elections' (arXiv:2604.19851) reports extensive SAT/computational search finding no election of dimension > 3 and states the gap 3 <= k <= 5 as open. Special cases: dimension <= 3 for l1 and l_inf metric elections (arXiv:2410.09201) and for planar Euclidean metric elections (arXiv:2608.27653). Closing the gap is a central question in committee selection and connects to approximately dominating sets (arXiv:2504.20372, arXiv:2608.06872).

literature.title: Optimal metric distortion of randomized ordinal voting rules
literature.statement: Voters $V$ ($|V|=n$) and candidates $C$ ($|C|=m$) lie in a common (pseudo)metric space $d$. Each voter reports a strict ranking of $C$ consistent with $d$ (if $d(v,a)<d(v,b)$ then $v$ ranks $a$ above $b$). A randomized ordinal rule $f$ maps each ranking profile $\sigma$ to a probability distribution over $C$. Social cost: $SC_d(c)=\sum_{v\in V} d(v,c)$. The distortion of $f$ is $\sup_{n,m,\sigma}\ \sup_{d \text{ consistent with } \sigma} \mathbb{E}_{c\sim f(\sigma)}[SC_d(c)] / \min_{c'} SC_d(c')$. Question: determine $\alpha^* = \inf_f \mathrm{dist}(f)$. Known: $2.1126 \le \alpha^* \le 2.13713$ (deterministic rules: optimal value is exactly 3).
literature.source_title: Metric Distortion Bounds for Randomized Social Choice
literature.rationale: A natural conjecture that randomized rules achieve distortion 2 was refuted by the lower bound approaching 2.1126 as the number of candidates grows ('Metric Distortion Bounds for Randomized Social Choice', arXiv:2111.03694). The first constant separation from 3 was 2.753 ('Breaking the Metric Voting Distortion Barrier', arXiv:2306.17838). In Aug-Sep 2026 the upper bound dropped rapidly: 5/2 ('An improved bound for the randomized metric distortion problem', arXiv:2608.17863), 2.1441 ('Improving Randomized Metric Distortion to 2.1441', arXiv:2608.29308), and 2.13713 ('Stable Voting Rules on the Edge of Optimal Metric Distortion', arXiv:2609.08259), within 0.025 of the lower bound. The exact optimum, and whether the lower-bound construction is tight, remain open. The m=3 case is resolved exactly in arXiv:2111.03694.

literature.title: Maximum size of a Condorcet domain
literature.statement: A Condorcet domain on the alternative set $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$ is a set $D$ of linear orders on $[n]$ such that for every finite profile of voters with an odd number of voters, each voter's order taken from $D$, the pairwise strict-majority relation is transitive. Equivalently, for every three alternatives $a,b,c$, the restrictions of the orders in $D$ to $\{a,b,c\}$ satisfy a never-condition: some $x\in\{a,b,c\}$ and some position $p\in\{1,2,3\}$ such that $x$ never appears at position $p$ in any restriction. Let $f(n)$ be the maximum $|D|$. Questions: (a) determine $f(9)$ (known $492 \le f(9)$); (b) determine $\lim_{n\to\infty} f(n)^{1/n}$ (known to be at least $2.198139$ and finite).
literature.source_title: Improved lower bounds for the maximum size of Condorcet domains
literature.location: Introduction (exact maximum only known for n <= 8)
literature.rationale: The maximum size of acyclic sets of linear orders is a classical question going back to the early 1990s literature on Condorcet domains. Exact values are known only up to n=8, where f(8)=224 with a unique extremal domain ('The Largest Condorcet Domains on 8 Alternatives', arXiv:2303.15002). Heuristic and supercomputer searches ('New Record-Breaking Condorcet Domains on 10 and 11 Alternatives', arXiv:2303.06524; arXiv:2601.07336) give f(9)>=492, f(10)>=1104, f(11)>=2452 and an asymptotic lower bound Omega(2.198139^n). An exponential upper bound c^n is known but with an implicit constant that gives no realistic value, so the growth rate is wide open. The n=9 case is a finite but very large search.

literature.title: Committee monotonicity versus EJR in approval-based committee voting
literature.statement: Let $N=\{1,\dots,n\}$ be voters and $C$ a finite set of $m$ candidates; voter $i$ approves a set $A_i\subseteq C$. For a committee size $k$, a group $G\subseteq N$ is $\ell$-cohesive if $|G|\ge \ell n/k$ and $|\bigcap_{i\in G}A_i|\ge \ell$. A committee $W\subseteq C$ with $|W|=k$ satisfies Extended Justified Representation (EJR) if for every $\ell\ge 1$ and every $\ell$-cohesive group $G$ there is $i\in G$ with $|A_i\cap W|\ge \ell$. Question: does every approval profile admit an ordering $c_1,c_2,\dots,c_m$ of all candidates such that for every $k\in\{1,\dots,m\}$ the prefix $\{c_1,\dots,c_k\}$ satisfies EJR for committee size $k$? (Equivalently: does there exist a resolute committee-monotonic approval-based committee rule satisfying EJR?)
literature.source_title: Multi-Winner Voting with Approval Preferences
literature.location: Open problems chapter, Q2 (Committee monotonicity and proportionality)
literature.rationale: Committee monotonicity (W(k) ⊆ W(k+1)) is essential for ranking candidates/excellence lists. Sequential Phragmén is committee monotonic and satisfies the weaker PJR, while all known EJR rules (PAV, Method of Equal Shares) violate committee monotonicity. The survey states no impossibility is known and only partial answers exist: a positive answer is known for approval-based party-list elections ('Approval-Based Apportionment', arXiv:1911.08365). Because a resolute rule may be defined profile-by-profile, the question is exactly the per-profile chain-existence statement above, so a counterexample is a finite object that could be found by SAT search; a positive answer would require a new construction.

literature.title: Do 2-approximately stable committees always exist?
literature.statement: There are $n$ voters and a finite candidate set $C$ with unit weights; a committee is a subset $S\subseteq C$. Each voter $v$ has a complete transitive (weak) preference $\succeq_v$ over all subsets of $C$ that is monotone: $S_1\subseteq S_2 \Rightarrow S_2\succeq_v S_1$. Fix a size limit $K\ge1$. For $c\ge1$, a committee $S$ with $|S|\le K$ is $c$-approximately stable if for every committee $S'$ (of any size $K'=|S'|$), the number of voters who strictly prefer $S'$ to $S$ is strictly less than $c\,\frac{K'}{K}\,n$. ($c=1$ is the core.) Question: for every such instance, does a 2-approximately stable committee exist? It is known that $c$ cannot be below 2 in general, and that $c=32$ always suffices (16 when exactly stable lotteries exist).
literature.source_title: Approximately Stable Committee Selection
literature.location: Sec. 5 (Open Questions), last bullet; companion question: exactly stable lotteries (first bullet)
literature.rationale: Stability (core) is the strongest group-fairness notion for committee selection and covers participatory budgeting, facility location and ranking-based committee voting as special cases. Exactly stable committees can fail to exist (cyclic preferences), and Appendix A of arXiv:1910.14008 shows (2-eps)-stable committees may fail to exist even in the ranking setting with unit weights; the same paper proves an O(1) bound (32, improvable to 16 when exactly stable lotteries exist, e.g. ranking and approval settings via 'Group Fairness in Committee Selection', arXiv:1905.04438) and conjectures 2 is tight. In the approval special case the constant has been driven to 2 ('Sequential Phragmén Guarantees 2-Approximate Core Stability', arXiv:2609.29646) and an exact core is claimed (arXiv:2609.11912), so the open frontier is general monotone and ranking preferences. Related open question from the same section: does an exactly stable lottery exist for all monotone preferences (known only for K <= 3)?

literature.title: Maximum number of stable matchings
literature.statement: A stable-marriage instance of size $n$ has $n$ men and $n$ women, each with a strict total order over all agents of the other side. A perfect matching is stable if no man-woman pair strictly prefer each other to their partners. Let $M(n)$ be the maximum, over all instances of size $n$, of the number of stable matchings. Since $M(a+b)\ge M(a)M(b)$, the limit $\beta=\lim_n M(n)^{1/n}$ exists. Question: determine $\beta$; known $2.28 \lesssim \beta \le 3.55$. In particular, is the classical lower-bound construction (base $\approx 2.28$) optimal?
literature.source_title: At most 3.55^n stable matchings
literature.rationale: One of the classical open questions on stable marriage from the 1970s literature. For decades the best upper bound was super-exponential; 'A Simply Exponential Upper Bound on the Maximum Number of Stable Matchings' (arXiv:1711.01032) gave c^n with a huge constant, and 'At most 3.55^n stable matchings' (arXiv:2011.00915) brought it to 3.55^n via an entropy method. The best lower bound, Omega(2.28^n), comes from a recursive construction for n a power of 2 and has stood since the 1980s. Exact M(n) is known only for small n.

literature.title: Approximately counting stable matchings (FPRAS)
literature.statement: Given a stable-marriage instance with $n$ men and $n$ women having complete strict preferences, let $\#SM$ be its number of stable matchings. Question: is there a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (FPRAS) for $\#SM$, i.e. a randomized algorithm that, given the instance and $\varepsilon>0$, outputs $Z$ with $\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)\#SM \le Z \le (1+\varepsilon)\#SM]\ge 3/4$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $1/\varepsilon$? This is equivalent (under approximation-preserving reductions) to the existence of an FPRAS for counting independent sets in bipartite graphs (#BIS); it is conjectured that none exists.
literature.source_title: The Complexity of Approximately Counting Stable Matchings
literature.rationale: Exact counting is #P-complete (classical, 1980s). Stable matchings correspond bijectively to downsets (closed sets) of the rotation poset, and every finite poset arises this way, so approximate counting is #BIS-equivalent; 'The Complexity of Approximately Counting Stable Matchings' (arXiv:1004.1836) shows equivalence persists even in restricted attribute models and identifies easy special cases. Resolving it either way would settle the #BIS question, one of the central open problems in approximate counting.

literature.title: Is computing an exact Hylland–Zeckhauser equilibrium FIXP-hard?
literature.statement: A Hylland–Zeckhauser (HZ) market has $n$ agents and $n$ goods, each good with unit supply, and nonnegative utilities $u_{ij}$; every agent has budget 1. An HZ equilibrium is a price vector $p\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n$ and a fractional allocation $x\in[0,1]^{n\times n}$ with $\sum_j x_{ij}=1$ for each agent and $\sum_i x_{ij}=1$ for each good, such that each row $x_i$ maximizes $\sum_j u_{ij}y_j$ over $\{y\ge0: \sum_j y_j=1, \sum_j p_j y_j\le 1\}$ and, among maximizers, minimizes cost $\sum_j p_j y_j$. Equilibria always exist (by a fixed-point argument) but may be irrational. Question: is the problem of computing an exact HZ equilibrium FIXP-hard (hence FIXP-complete, since membership in FIXP is known)?
literature.source_title: Computational Complexity of the Hylland-Zeckhauser Scheme for One-Sided Matching Markets
literature.location: Abstract and Sec. 1 ('We leave open the problem of determining if HZ is FIXP-hard')
literature.rationale: The HZ scheme is the canonical pricing-based mechanism for one-sided matching with cardinal utilities. arXiv:2004.01348 shows equilibria can be irrational and puts the problem in FIXP; 'Computational Hardness of the Hylland-Zeckhauser Scheme' (arXiv:2107.05746) proves PPAD-hardness of computing approximate equilibria (even with 4-valued utilities), settling the approximate case, but leaves exact FIXP-completeness and the 3-valued-utility case open. 'Hardness of approximate Hylland-Zeckhauser equilibria' (arXiv:2606.00951, 2026) extends approximate hardness conditionally. The exact case remains open; few natural market problems are known to be FIXP-complete.

literature.title: Core of simple symmetric fractional hedonic games on bipartite graphs
literature.statement: Let $G=(N,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph. In the associated simple symmetric fractional hedonic game, a partition $\pi$ of $N$ gives each player $i$ utility $u_i(\pi(i)) = |\{j\in \pi(i): \{i,j\}\in E\}| / |\pi(i)|$, where $\pi(i)$ is $i$'s block. A nonempty coalition $S\subseteq N$ blocks $\pi$ if $u_i(S) > u_i(\pi(i))$ for every $i\in S$; $\pi$ is in the core if no coalition blocks it. Question: if $G$ is bipartite, is the core always nonempty?
literature.source_title: Fractional Hedonic Games
literature.rationale: For general simple symmetric fractional hedonic games the core can be empty (a 40-player example in arXiv:1705.10116) and deciding non-emptiness is computationally hard. Non-emptiness is known for graphs of maximum degree at most 2, forests, complete multipartite graphs, graphs of girth at least 5, bipartite graphs with a perfect matching, and regular bipartite graphs; the K_{4,10} example shows star-packing methods that work for girth >= 5 fail for bipartite graphs. Bipartite graphs (girth >= 4) are the natural boundary case. A counterexample would be a finite graph, so computer search plus Lean verification is plausible; a positive proof needs a new idea.

literature.title: Constant-Factor Truthful Mechanism for XOS/Submodular Combinatorial Auctions
literature.statement: There are $n$ bidders and a set $M$ of $m$ items. Each bidder $i$ has a private valuation $v_i:2^M\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ with $v_i(\emptyset)=0$. It is monotone and XOS, meaning $v_i(S)=\max_{\ell} \sum_{j\in S} a^{i}_{\ell j}$ for finitely many nonnegative additive clauses $a^i_\ell$. Submodular valuations are a special case. A mechanism learns about valuations only through value queries ($S\mapsto v_i(S)$) and demand queries (prices $p\in\mathbb{R}^M_{\ge0}\mapsto$ some $S\in\arg\max_S v_i(S)-\sum_{j\in S}p_j$). It may use at most $\mathrm{poly}(n,m)$ queries and computation. It outputs a partition of items to bidders and payments. It is universally truthful if it is a probability distribution over deterministic mechanisms in each of which truthful reporting is a dominant strategy for every bidder. Its approximation ratio is $\sup_{v} \mathrm{OPT}(v)/\mathbb{E}[\sum_i v_i(A_i)]$. Question: is there a universally truthful (or at least truthful-in-expectation) mechanism of this kind whose approximation ratio is $O(1)$, independent of $n$ and $m$? Equivalently, can truthful mechanisms match the constant-factor approximation that non-truthful polynomial-query algorithms achieve?
literature.source_title: Improved Truthful Mechanisms for Subadditive Combinatorial Auctions: Breaking the Logarithmic Barrier
literature.rationale: This is the central open problem on the price of truthfulness in combinatorial auctions. Without incentives, constant factors are easy: $1-1/e$ for XOS with demand queries. Truthful mechanisms went from $O(\log m\log\log m)$ and $O(\sqrt{\log m})$ to $O((\log\log m)^3)$ for submodular/XOS bidders (arXiv:1911.02716) and to $O((\log\log m)^3)$ for subadditive bidders (arXiv:2010.01420). With value queries alone, polynomially many queries provably cannot give better than an $m^{\Omega(1)}$ ratio (see the discussion in arXiv:1911.02716 and 'Limitations of randomized mechanisms for combinatorial auctions', arXiv:1109.1055). The demand-query case is wide open: no super-constant lower bound for truthful mechanisms is known, and no communication separation between truthful mechanisms and algorithms is known either.

literature.title: Optimal Truthful-in-Expectation Mechanism for Unrelated-Machine Scheduling
literature.statement: There are $n$ machines and $m$ jobs. Machine $i$ privately knows its processing times $t_i=(t_{i1},\dots,t_{im})\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^m$. A randomized mechanism maps a reported profile $t$ to a probability distribution over assignments $\sigma:[m]\to[n]$ and to payments $P_i(t)$. Machine $i$'s expected utility is $P_i(t)-\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i} t_{ij}]$ when evaluated at its true times. The mechanism is truthful in expectation (TIE) if no machine can raise its expected utility by misreporting, whatever the others report. Its approximation ratio is $\rho=\sup_t \mathbb{E}_\sigma[\max_i \sum_{j:\sigma(j)=i} t_{ij}] / \mathrm{OPT}(t)$, where $\mathrm{OPT}(t)$ is the minimum makespan. Question: determine $\rho^*_{\mathrm{TIE}}(n)=\inf$ over TIE mechanisms of $\rho$. Is it bounded by a constant, or does it grow linearly in $n$? The case $n=2$ is also open: find the exact optimal ratio for two machines.
literature.source_title: A proof of the Nisan-Ronen conjecture
literature.rationale: The deterministic Nisan–Ronen conjecture (ratio $n$) was proved in arXiv:2301.11905, so randomization is now the main open question in truthful scheduling. Known bounds: $2-1/n\le\rho^*_{\mathrm{TIE}}(n)\le (n+5)/2$, and fractional mechanisms achieve $(n+1)/2$. For universally truthful mechanisms, 'Universally truthful mechanisms for scheduling' (arXiv:2609.12621) shows a lower bound of $n/12-o(n)$ for discrete-support mechanisms and an upper bound of $n/2+o(n)$. That separates them from the TIE question, which is still open. For $n=2$ the bounds are $1.5$ and about $1.587$ ('Copula-based Randomized Mechanisms for Truthful Scheduling on Two Unrelated Machines', arXiv:1306.3909).

literature.title: Optimal Competitive Ratio for Prophet Secretary
literature.statement: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions $F_1,\dots,F_n$. A uniformly random permutation $\pi$ is drawn and the values are revealed in the order $X_{\pi(1)},X_{\pi(2)},\dots$. After each value is revealed, an online algorithm must irrevocably either stop and receive that value or continue. It may use the distributions, the past values and the identities of the variables seen so far. Let $\alpha^*=\inf_{n,F_1,\dots,F_n}\sup_{\mathrm{ALG}} \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}]/\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]$. Question: determine $\alpha^*$. Known: $0.688\le\alpha^*\le 0.7235$.
literature.source_title: Prophet Secretary
literature.rationale: This is the canonical random-order prophet inequality. It sits between the adversarial-order prophet inequality, where $1/2$ is tight, and the i.i.d. case, where the constant $\approx0.745$ is tight. The original paper (arXiv:1507.01155) gave $1-1/e$. 'Prophet Secretary and Matching: the Significance of the Largest Item' (arXiv:2411.01191) gives $0.688$, beating the $0.675$ barrier for blind strategies. 'Prophet Inequalities: Separating Random Order from Order Selection' (arXiv:2304.04024) gives the upper bound $0.7235$. The gap is still about $0.035$.

literature.title: Free-Order (Order-Selection) Prophet Inequality Constant
literature.statement: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be independent nonnegative random variables with known distributions. Before any value is revealed, the gambler chooses a permutation $\pi$ (it may depend on the distributions). Values $X_{\pi(1)},X_{\pi(2)},\dots$ are then revealed one by one and the gambler stops irrevocably at most once, receiving the current value. Let $\beta^*=\inf_{n,F}\sup_{\pi,\tau}\mathbb{E}[X_{\pi(\tau)}]/\mathbb{E}[\max_i X_i]$, where $\tau$ ranges over stopping times. Let $\gamma\approx0.7451$ be the i.i.d. prophet constant: the unique $\gamma$ with $\int_0^1 \big(y(1-\ln y)+1/\gamma-1\big)^{-1}dy=1$. Then $\beta^*\le\gamma$. Question: is $\beta^*=\gamma$, i.e., is the worst case for free order attained by i.i.d. instances? Known: $0.7258\le\beta^*\le\gamma$.
literature.source_title: Order Selection Prophet Inequality: From Threshold Optimization to Arrival Time Design
literature.rationale: This is a natural and well-known question: does the power to choose the order fully recover the i.i.d. guarantee? 'Order Selection Prophet Inequality: From Threshold Optimization to Arrival Time Design' (arXiv:2204.01425) raised the lower bound from 0.669 to 0.725. 'Prophet Inequality: Order selection beats random order' (arXiv:2211.04145) gives 0.7258. 'Prophet Inequalities: Separating Random Order from Order Selection' (arXiv:2304.04024) shows random order is strictly worse (at most 0.7235). It is open whether $\beta^*$ equals $\approx0.745$.

literature.title: Exact Approximation Ratio of the Random-Offerer Mechanism
literature.statement: There is one seller with value $s\sim F_S$ and one buyer with value $b\sim F_B$, drawn independently with known distributions on $\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$. In the seller-offering mechanism, the seller posts $p_S(s)\in\arg\max_p (p-s)(1-F_B(p))$ and trade happens iff $b\ge p_S(s)$. In the buyer-offering mechanism, the buyer posts $p_B(b)\in\arg\max_p (b-p)F_S(p)$ and trade happens iff $s\le p_B(b)$. The random-offerer mechanism (RO) runs each with probability $1/2$. Its gains from trade are $\mathrm{RO}=\mathbb{E}[(b-s)\mathbf 1_{\text{trade}}]$, and $\mathrm{FB}=\mathbb{E}[(b-s)^+]$. Question: determine $R^*=\sup_{F_S,F_B}\mathrm{FB}/\mathrm{RO}$. Known: $2.1728\lesssim R^*\le\pi$. Ties in the argmax may be broken in favour of trade.
literature.source_title: Approximately Efficient Bilateral Trade
literature.rationale: The second-best ratio is now settled at exactly $1/2$ ('Second-Best Bilateral Trade is 1/2 Efficient', arXiv:2606.03849). The tight constant for the simplest dominant-strategy, budget-balanced, IR mechanism is still unknown. The upper bound on $R^*$ went from $8.23$ (arXiv:2111.03611) to $3.15$ ('Improved Approximation to First-Best Gains-from-Trade', arXiv:2205.00140; also 'A Geometric Analysis of Gains from Trade', arXiv:2508.06469) to $\pi$ ('Tighter Bounds for the Random-Offerer Mechanism in Bilateral Trade', arXiv:2607.13959). Lower-bound instances give $2.0749$ ('A New Lower Bound for the Random Offerer Mechanism in Bilateral Trade using AI-Guided Evolutionary Search', arXiv:2603.08679) and about $2.1728$ (arXiv:2607.13959). This kind of question is well suited to explicit-instance certificates in Lean.

literature.title: Strong Matroid Secretary Conjecture (1/e for Every Matroid)
literature.statement: Let $M=(E,\mathcal I)$ be a matroid on $n$ elements with distinct (adversarial) weights $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$. Elements arrive in a uniformly random order. On arrival of an element, the algorithm learns how it compares in weight with all previously arrived elements (ordinal model), or its weight. It may query independence of subsets of arrived elements and must irrevocably accept or reject it, keeping the accepted set in $\mathcal I$. Conjecture: for every matroid there is such an algorithm with $\mathbb{E}[w(\mathrm{ALG})]\ge \frac1e\, w(\mathrm{OPT})$. A stronger form asks that every element of the max-weight basis $\mathrm{OPT}$ is accepted with probability $\ge 1/e$. The constant $1/e$ would be best possible, as the rank-1 uniform matroid (classical secretary problem) shows.
literature.source: Matroids, Secretary Problems, and Online Mechanisms (SODA 2007); restated as Conjecture 1.1 in arXiv:2609.19118
literature.source_title: Matroids, Secretary Problems, and Online Mechanisms
literature.rationale: The constant-ratio matroid secretary conjecture was claimed resolved in September 2026 ('The Matroid Secretary Conjecture is True', arXiv:2609.14555, ratio $1/4$; improved to $1/3.1462$ in arXiv:2609.17782). The sharp constant $1/e$ is the remaining well-known target. 'On the Strong Matroid Secretary Conjecture and Beyond' (arXiv:2609.19118) and 'The Strong Secretary Conjecture is True for Linear Matroids' (arXiv:2609.20797) prove it for linear matroids. These cover graphic, regular and transversal matroids and gammoids. General matroids are open, and so are non-representable families such as sparse paving matroids.

literature.title: Polynomial-Time ε-Nash Equilibria for Bimatrix Games with ε < 1/3
literature.statement: A bimatrix game is a pair of matrices $A,B\in[0,1]^{n\times n}$ with rational entries. A pair of mixed strategies $(x,y)$ in the simplices $\Delta_n\times\Delta_n$ is an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium if $x^\top A y\ge \max_i (Ay)_i-\varepsilon$ and $x^\top B y\ge \max_j (x^\top B)_j-\varepsilon$. Question: is there a constant $\varepsilon<1/3$ and a polynomial-time algorithm (in the bit size of $A,B$) that outputs an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium of every bimatrix game?
literature.source_title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for 1/3-Approximate Nash Equilibria in Bimatrix Games
literature.rationale: Computing exact Nash equilibria is PPAD-complete. Polynomial-time approximation progressed through $3/4, 1/2, 0.38, 0.36, 0.3393$, and then $1/3+\delta$ ('A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for 1/3-Approximate Nash Equilibria in Bimatrix Games', arXiv:2204.11525). On the hardness side, 'Settling the complexity of computing approximate two-player Nash equilibria' (arXiv:1606.04550) shows that, under ETH for PPAD, some small constant $\varepsilon$ needs $n^{\log^{1-o(1)}n}$ time. A quasi-polynomial algorithm exists for every constant $\varepsilon$. Whether $1/3$ is a natural barrier for polynomial time is open, and so is what the true threshold is.

literature.title: Query Complexity of Tarski Fixed Points on the Grid
literature.statement: For $n,k\ge1$, let $L=[n]^k$ with the componentwise partial order, where $[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}$. TARSKI$(n,k)$ is the problem: given oracle access to a monotone map $f:L\to L$ ($x\le y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y)$), find some $x$ with $f(x)=x$. One exists by Tarski's theorem. Let $Q(n,k)$ be the deterministic query complexity (worst-case number of oracle calls). Questions: (a) is $Q(n,k)=O(\log^2 n)$ for every fixed $k$? In particular, is $Q(n,5)=O(\log^2 n)$? (b) Is $Q(n,k)\le \mathrm{poly}(k,\log n)$, i.e., with an exponent of $\log n$ independent of $k$? (c) In the white-box model, where $f$ is given by a Boolean circuit, can a fixed point be found in polynomial time?
literature.source_title: Tarski's Theorem, Supermodular Games, and the Complexity of Equilibria
literature.rationale: Tarski fixed points capture equilibria of supermodular games and several stochastic game problems, and lie in PLS ∩ PPAD. Known bounds: $Q(n,k)=\Theta(\log^2 n)$ for $k=2,3,4$. The $k=4$ case and the bound $O(\log^{\lceil (k-1)/3\rceil+1} n)$ for general $k$ are from 'The Mystery Deepens: On the Query Complexity of Tarski Fixed Points' (arXiv:2604.00268). The earlier $O(\log^{\lceil (k+1)/2\rceil}n)$ is from 'A faster algorithm for finding Tarski fixed points' (arXiv:2010.02618) and successors. The best lower bound is $\Omega(k\log^2 n/\log k)$, even for randomized algorithms ('Tarski Lower Bounds from Multi-Dimensional Herringbones', arXiv:2502.16679). Whether the complexity grows with dimension at all beyond the $k$ factor is open; the field calls this a mystery.

literature.title: Are Simple Stochastic Games Solvable in Polynomial Time?
literature.statement: A simple stochastic game (SSG) is a finite directed graph whose vertices are partitioned into MAX, MIN and AVERAGE vertices, plus two sink vertices, $0$-sink and $1$-sink. Every non-sink vertex has two out-edges. A token moves from a start vertex. MAX (resp. MIN) chooses the successor at MAX (resp. MIN) vertices, and at AVERAGE vertices the successor is chosen uniformly at random. MAX wins if the token reaches the $1$-sink. The value $v(u)$ is the probability that MAX wins from $u$ under optimal play. It exists, and positional (memoryless deterministic) optimal strategies exist. Question: is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an SSG and a vertex $u$, decides whether $v(u)>1/2$ (equivalently, computes all values exactly as rationals)?
literature.source: The Complexity of Stochastic Games (Information and Computation 96(2), 1992)
literature.source_title: The Complexity of Stochastic Games
literature.rationale: This is a famous problem in NP ∩ coNP that is not known to be in P. Parity, mean-payoff and discounted games all reduce to it in polynomial time. The best algorithms are randomized subexponential ($2^{O(\sqrt n)}$) or fixed-parameter in the number of AVERAGE vertices. Strategy-improvement methods have exponential lower bounds. Stopping SSGs lie in UEOPL ('Unique End of Potential Line', arXiv:1811.03841). 'Reducing Stochastic Games to Semidefinite Programming' (arXiv:2411.09646) gives a polynomial reduction to SDP feasibility, but SDP feasibility is not known to be in P.

literature.title: Are Parity Games Solvable in Polynomial Time?
literature.statement: A parity game is a finite directed graph $G=(V,E)$ where every vertex has at least one successor. $V=V_0\sqcup V_1$ is partitioned between players Even and Odd, and there is a priority function $p:V\to\{0,\dots,d\}$. From a start vertex, the owner of the current vertex picks a successor, forever. The resulting infinite play is won by Even iff $\max\{p(v): v \text{ occurs infinitely often}\}$ is even. Parity games are positionally determined. Question: is there an algorithm that, given $(G,p)$ and a vertex $v$, decides which player has a winning strategy from $v$ in time polynomial in $|V|+|E|$ (with $d\le|V|$)?
literature.source: Deciding Parity Games in Quasipolynomial Time (STOC 2017)
literature.source_title: Deciding Parity Games in Quasipolynomial Time
literature.rationale: This is the central open problem of infinite-duration games and the algorithmic core of μ-calculus model checking and LTL synthesis. It is in NP ∩ coNP and UP ∩ coUP. Since 2017 there have been quasi-polynomial algorithms ($n^{O(\log d)}$), e.g. 'An Ordered Approach to Solving Parity Games in Quasi Polynomial Time and Quasi Linear Space' (arXiv:1703.01296). 'Universal trees grow inside separating automata: Quasi-polynomial lower bounds for parity games' (arXiv:1807.10546) shows that every separating-automaton approach is inherently quasi-polynomial. A November 2025 preprint (arXiv:2511.03752) claims a polynomial algorithm, but it has not been validated by the community.

literature.title: Sylver Coinage After the Opening Move 16
literature.statement: Sylver coinage is a two-player game. Players alternately name a positive integer that is not a sum of nonnegative integer multiples of the integers named so far. The player who names $1$ loses. Equivalently, $1$ is excluded and a player with no other legal move loses. Every play is finite, so every position is either a first-player win (N) or a second-player win (P). Question: after the first player opens with $16$, does the player to move (the second player) have a winning reply? That is, is the position $\{16\}$ an N-position or a P-position? If it is N, which replies win?
literature.source: Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays (Vol. 3, 2nd ed.); also 'Unsolved Problems in Combinatorial Games' (Games of No Chance, MSRI Publ. 29, 1996)
literature.source_title: Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays
literature.rationale: This is a famous prize problem in combinatorial game theory. All openings below $16$ have known outcomes, and every prime $p\ge5$ is a known winning opening (a classical theorem on 'ender' primes). The game has infinitely many options until the named set has gcd $1$, so plain search does not apply directly. Positions with gcd $1$ reduce to numerical semigroups with finitely many gaps. Recent computational campaigns (2025-2026) have certified hundreds of thousands of sub-positions under $\{16\}$, but they report that the opening remains undecided.

literature.title: Periodicity of Grundy's Game
literature.statement: In Grundy's game a position is a multiset of heap sizes. A move picks one heap of size $n$ and splits it into two nonempty heaps of different sizes $a+b=n$, $a\ne b$. A player with no move loses (normal play). The Grundy value of a single heap is $g(n)=\operatorname{mex}\{g(a)\oplus g(b): a+b=n,\ 1\le a<b\}$, where $\oplus$ is bitwise XOR and $g(1)=g(2)=0$. Question: is the sequence $g$ eventually periodic, i.e., are there $N$ and $p\ge1$ with $g(n+p)=g(n)$ for all $n\ge N$?
literature.source: Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays
literature.source_title: Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays
literature.rationale: Grundy's game is the best-known test case for (non-)periodicity of impartial heap games. It is conjectured to be eventually periodic. Very long computations (the first $2^{35}$ values have been reported) show no period, but the values grow very slowly and show strong structure, e.g. almost all values are $0,1,2$ mod small patterns. No proof technique is known in either direction.

literature.title: Guy's Conjecture: Finite Octal Games Are Eventually Periodic
literature.statement: A finite octal game is given by a code $0.d_1d_2\dots d_k$ with digits $d_j\in\{0,\dots,7\}$. On a position (a multiset of heaps), a move takes one heap of size $h$ and removes $j\le h$ tokens from it. The remainder $h-j$ is left as zero heaps if bit $1$ of $d_j$ is set (requires $h=j$). It is left as one nonempty heap if bit $2$ is set (requires $h>j$). It is left as two nonempty heaps $a+b=h-j$, $a,b\ge1$, if bit $4$ is set. Under normal play, the single-heap Grundy values are $G(h)=\operatorname{mex}$ of $G(h-j)$ (bit 2), of $0$ (bit 1, $h=j$) and of $G(a)\oplus G(b)$ (bit 4). Conjecture: for every finite octal code, the sequence $G$ is eventually periodic. The smallest unresolved examples include $0.007$.
literature.source: Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays; 'Unsolved Problems in Combinatorial Games' (Games of No Chance, MSRI Publ. 29, 1996)
literature.source_title: Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays
literature.rationale: This is the central conjecture of impartial heap games. The octal periodicity theorem makes eventual periodicity checkable for a single game once a long enough periodic stretch is observed. Many octal games have been settled this way, but several small codes ($0.007$ and others) show no period after hundreds of millions of values. Proving it for even a single such game, or finding a non-periodic finite octal game, would be a landmark.

literature.title: Hex: Classify All Opening Moves on the 10×10 Board
literature.statement: Hex on an $n\times n$ rhombic board of hexagonal cells: Black owns the top and bottom sides and White owns the left and right sides. Players alternately place a stone of their colour on an empty cell, with Black moving first. A player wins on forming a connected chain of their stones joining their two sides. Draws are impossible, and the first player wins on an empty board, by a non-constructive strategy-stealing argument. For each cell $c$, let $\mathrm{Win}_n(c)$ mean that Black, after opening at $c$, has a winning strategy (with White to move next and no swap rule). Question: determine $\mathrm{Win}_{10}(c)$ for all 100 cells $c$. More ambitiously, exhibit any explicit winning opening and strategy on the $11\times11$ board.
literature.source: Scalable Parallel DFPN Search (Computers and Games 2013, LNCS 8427)
literature.source_title: Scalable Parallel DFPN Search
literature.rationale: Hex is the classical example of a game where strategy stealing proves a first-player win without a strategy. Every opening is solved for $n\le9$, while for $n=10$ only a handful are, including the centre. Nothing is known constructively for the standard $11\times11$ board. Progress is purely computational (proof-number search with virtual-connection and inferior-cell pruning), which makes certificate-checking in a proof assistant an interesting, if very large, target.

literature.title: The Sprouts Conjecture
literature.statement: Sprouts starts with $n$ spots in the plane. A move draws a simple curve joining two spots, or a spot to itself, that crosses no existing curve or spot. The player then places a new spot on the interior of the new curve. Each spot may be the endpoint of at most three curve-ends; a loop counts twice. A player unable to move loses (normal play). The game always ends within $3n-1$ moves. Conjecture: the first player has a winning strategy in $n$-spot Sprouts iff $n\equiv 3,4,5 \pmod 6$.
literature.source: Computer Analysis of Sprouts (Carnegie Mellon Univ. tech. report CMU-CS-91-144, 1991); Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays
literature.source_title: Computer Analysis of Sprouts
literature.rationale: This is a well-known conjecture about a famous topological game, and it is supported by massive computation. Outcomes are known for all $n\le62$ plus 27 larger cases up to $n=104$ ('Massively Parallel Proof-Number Search for Impartial Games and Beyond', arXiv:2511.10339), up from $n\le 44$ with a few sporadic larger values (earlier work, e.g. 'Computer analysis of Sprouts with nimbers', arXiv:1008.2320). There is no theoretical approach to the mod-6 pattern.

literature.title: The Shield-Core conjecture for stable marriage
literature.statement: Consider the stable marriage problem with n men and n women and strict, complete preference lists. For a preference profile S let beta(S) be the largest number of blocking pairs of a complete matching of S, and let the shield number sigma(n) be the minimum of beta(S) over all such profiles. The cyclic Hollow-Shell profile C_n has man g rank woman h at position ((h - g) mod n) + 1 and woman h rank man g at position n - ((h - g) mod n). Is sigma(n) = beta(C_n) = floor((n - 1)^2 / 4) for every n? Equivalently: (a) every complete matching of C_n has at most floor((n - 1)^2 / 4) blocking pairs, and (b) every profile has a complete matching with at least floor((n - 1)^2 / 4) blocking pairs.
literature.source_title: A Quadratic Lower Bound for the Shield Number of the Stable Marriage Problem: Rearrangement, Extremal Construction, and Biclique Realizability
literature.location: Sec. 1.1 (Shield-Core conjecture); Sec. 7.1 and Sec. 8 (the upper bound on beta(C_n) is left open)
literature.rationale: The paper proves sigma(n) >= ceil(n(n - 2)/6) by a rearrangement argument and constructs a matching of C_n with exactly floor((n - 1)^2/4) blocking pairs (Theorem 5.3). It explicitly does not claim the upper bound beta(C_n) <= floor((n - 1)^2/4) or the exact equality; a related Hall-type biclique property is verified exhaustively for n <= 4.

literature.title: Weakly consecutive sequences begin or end with 1
literature.statement: A permutation sigma of {1, ..., k} is weakly consecutive if for all positions i, j and all integers m, whenever m divides sigma(i) and m divides i - j, then m divides sigma(j). Does every weakly consecutive sequence satisfy sigma(1) = 1 or sigma(k) = 1?
literature.source_title: Weakly Consecutive Sequences
literature.rationale: The paper generates weakly consecutive sequences from four starting sequences by three rules and conjectures that these produce every such sequence (Conjecture 5.1), which would imply this statement; the authors report that they could not prove it directly from the definition.

literature.title: Does MXS imply EEF1 for additive goods?
literature.statement: Notation as in the source: n agents, a set M of indivisible goods, valuations v_i with v_i(empty) = 0. An allocation is MXS-fair to agent i (minimum EFX share) if v_i(A_i) >= v_i(B_i) for some allocation B that is EFX-fair to i. An allocation A is EEF1-fair (epistemic EF1) to agent i if there is an allocation B with B_i = A_i that is EF1-fair to i, i.e. for every j there is a good g in B_j with v_i(B_i) >= v_i(B_j minus g). For additive goods and equal entitlements, is every allocation that is MXS-fair to agent i also EEF1-fair to agent i?
literature.source_title: Exploring Relations among Fairness Notions in Discrete Fair Division
literature.rationale: The implication holds for two agents (Lemma 22 of the source). Its inference engine settles almost every other implication among the 22 notions in this setting; this is the one left unresolved there.

literature.title: Does APS imply PROP1 for additive goods with unequal entitlements?
literature.statement: Additive goods, entitlements w_i > 0 summing to 1. Agent i's AnyPrice share is APS_i = min over price vectors p in R^m of the max of v_i(S) over bundles S with p(S) <= w_i p(M); an allocation is APS-fair to i if v_i(A_i) >= APS_i. It is PROP1-fair to i if v_i(A_i) >= w_i v_i(M), or v_i(A_i plus g) > w_i v_i(M) for some good g not in A_i (the source uses strict inequality). Is every allocation that is APS-fair to agent i also PROP1-fair to agent i?
literature.source_title: Exploring Relations among Fairness Notions in Discrete Fair Division
literature.rationale: The source maps implications among 22 fairness notions with an inference engine; for additive goods with unequal entitlements this implication is left open, even for two agents.

literature.title: Does MXS imply PROP1 for submodular goods?
literature.statement: Notation as in the source: n agents, a set M of indivisible goods, valuations v_i with v_i(empty) = 0. An allocation is MXS-fair to agent i (minimum EFX share) if v_i(A_i) >= v_i(B_i) for some allocation B that is EFX-fair to i. An allocation is PROP1-fair to i if v_i(A_i) >= v_i(M)/n or v_i(A_i plus g) > v_i(M)/n for some good g not in A_i. For monotone submodular valuations over goods and equal entitlements, is every allocation that is MXS-fair to agent i also PROP1-fair to agent i?
literature.source_title: Exploring Relations among Fairness Notions in Discrete Fair Division
literature.rationale: The implication holds for submodular valuations with binary marginals (Lemma 68 of the source).

literature.title: Does pairwise MMS imply MMS for submodular goods with binary marginals?
literature.statement: Equal entitlements, n agents, valuations submodular with binary marginals (v_i(S plus g) - v_i(S) in {0, 1}). Agent i's maximin share MMS_i is the max over partitions of M into n bundles of the min bundle value. An allocation is pairwise-MMS-fair to i if for every other agent j, A_i is worth at least i's 2-agent maximin share of A_i union A_j. Is every allocation that is pairwise-MMS-fair to every agent also MMS-fair to every agent?
literature.source_title: Exploring Relations among Fairness Notions in Discrete Fair Division
literature.rationale: The source maps implications among 22 fairness notions; for submodular goods with binary marginals this implication is one of the four it could not resolve.

literature.title: Swing rigidity of weighted voting games
literature.statement: For a simple game on n players and a player i, the swing table entry T(i, k) is the number of coalitions S of size k not containing i such that S is losing and S plus i is winning. Is every weighted voting game determined by its swing table among all simple games, i.e. if f is weighted and g is any simple game with the same swing table, must f = g?
literature.source_title: What Semivalues Cannot See: The Information Content of Anonymous Marginal Values
literature.location: Conjecture 10.2 (Sec. 10); first of the open problems in Sec. 11
literature.rationale: Distinct non-weighted simple games can share a swing table, so semivalues cannot tell them apart. An exhaustive census at n = 5 and searches at n = 6, 7 found no weighted game sharing its swing table with another game.

literature.title: Are the RAT-degree bounds 3 and 5 for deferred acceptance tight?
literature.statement: In a mechanism with agent set N, a manipulation by agent a_i is safe given known agents K and their preferences if it is weakly better than truth for every preference profile of the unknown agents, and profitable if it is strictly better for some. The RAT-degree is the least k such that some agent, for some k-set of known agents and some preferences of theirs, has a safe and profitable manipulation (n if none). For men-proposing deferred acceptance, with women as potential manipulators, the source shows RAT-degree at most 3 when truncation is allowed and at most 5 when only complete rankings may be reported. Are these bounds tight, i.e. is the RAT-degree exactly 3 with truncation and exactly 5 without truncation?
literature.source_title: It’s Not All Black and White: Degree of Truthfulness for Risk-Avoiding Agents
literature.rationale: Lemmas 8.2 and 8.3 give safe profitable manipulations with 3 known agents (truncation) and 5 known agents (reordering only); Lemma 8.5 shows no agent has a safe manipulation with no knowledge, so the RAT-degree is at least 1.

literature.title: Exact subsidy for envy-free orientations of multigraphs
literature.statement: Agents are the vertices of a multigraph and items are its edges; each edge can only go to one of its two endpoints (an orientation). Valuations are monotone, an agent values only edges incident to her, and the largest marginal value of any edge is at most 1. What is the worst-case minimum total subsidy needed to make some orientation envy-free, as a function of the number n of agents? The known bounds are n - 2 (lower) and n - 1 (upper).
literature.source_title: On the Subsidy of Envy-Free Orientations in Graphs
literature.location: Sec. 1.1 (Table 1) and Sec. 7, first open problem
literature.rationale: A total subsidy of n - 1 always suffices (Theorem 9), and a simple-graph instance needs n - 2 (Example 20), which is tight for simple graphs (Theorem 21). For additive valuations on multigraphs the answer is n/2.

literature.title: EF1 and Pareto optimality for connected chores on a path
literature.statement: Indivisible chores are arranged on a path and each agent must receive a connected bundle (an interval); costs are additive and strictly positive. An allocation is EF1 if for every agents i, j, removing some chore from i's bundle makes i not envy j. Pareto optimality is taken among connected allocations. Does a connected allocation that is both EF1 and Pareto optimal always exist?
literature.source_title: Connected EF1 Allocations Exist in Discrete Chore Cutting
literature.rationale: Connected EF1 (even EF1outer) allocations of chores always exist for monotone costs (the source's main result). Without connectivity, EF1 and PO are compatible for additive chores.

literature.title: Existence of PROPm orientations
literature.statement: In the orientation model, items (goods) are edges of a multigraph whose vertices are the agents, each item is relevant only to its two endpoints and must be given to one of them. An agent's proportional share is the sum over relevant items e of v_i(e)/n_e, where n_e = 2 is the number of agents to whom e is relevant. PROPm relaxes proportionality by the minimax-item slack (between PROP1 and PROPX). Does every instance with nonnegative additive valuations admit a PROPm orientation?
literature.source_title: Fair Orientations: Proportionality and Equitability
literature.rationale: PROP1 orientations always exist for goods on multigraphs, while PROPX orientations need not exist and deciding their existence is NP-complete (results of the source).

literature.title: Sybil-proof, ex-post safe procurement without winner-take-all equilibria
literature.statement: A buyer procures one unit of divisible work from agents with private linear costs c_i; a mechanism maps bids (an agent may submit several bids under different identities) to allocations x_i and payments p_i, with utility p_i - c_i x_i. It is Sybil-proof if every multi-bid strategy is weakly dominated by a single-bid strategy, and ex-post safe if each agent has a bidding strategy guaranteeing nonnegative utility against all others' bids and positive utility against some. Is there a procurement mechanism that is Sybil-proof and ex-post safe and whose pure Nash equilibria (under complete information) are not winner-take-all, i.e. give work to at least two agents?
literature.source_title: Beyond Winner-Take-All Procurement Auctions
literature.rationale: In the source, the DSIC proportional mechanism is not Sybil-proof, Tullock contests are Sybil-proof but not ex-post safe, and the paid-as-bid mechanism is ex-post safe but not Sybil-proof.

literature.title: Concavity of the QA weight-score without convex exposure
literature.statement: Given a proper scoring rule s and expert forecasts p_1..p_m, the quasi-arithmetic (QA) pool with weights w averages the forecasts in the exposure (gradient) space of s. Theorem 5.1 of the source shows that if s has convex exposure, then for every outcome j the weight-score WS_j(w) = s(QA pool of (p_i, w_i); j) is concave in w. Does this concavity hold for every proper scoring rule, without the convex-exposure assumption?
literature.source_title: From Proper Scoring Rules to Max-Min Optimal Forecast Aggregation
literature.location: Sec. 7 (Conclusions and future work), third bullet
literature.rationale: Every proper scoring rule for binary outcomes has convex exposure, as do the logarithmic and quadratic rules and several power families (App. D), so a counterexample needs at least three outcomes and a rule outside these classes.

literature.title: Optimal receiver-utility constant in bit-string persuasion
literature.statement: The state is a bit string X drawn from a prior mu; a sender observes X and commits to a signaling scheme; the receiver guesses every bit and is paid the number of correct guesses; the sender wants as many bits as possible guessed as 1. Let R_0(mu) be the receiver's utility from the prior alone and R_max(mu) the largest receiver utility among sender-optimal schemes. What is the least constant c such that R_max(mu) <= c R_0(mu) for every prior mu?
literature.source_title: Quantifying Theoretical AI Alignment Guarantees: Receiver-Utility Bounds in Bayesian Persuasion
literature.rationale: The source proves c <= 3/2 (Theorem 4.5) and gives a six-bit prior with ratio 39/31 > 5/4, so the optimal constant lies in [39/31, 3/2].

literature.title: Does the Monroe rule satisfy Droop-JR when k does not divide n?
literature.statement: Approval-based committee elections with n voters and committee size k. The Hare Monroe rule assigns each winner a group of about n/k voters and maximizes the number of voters who approve their assigned winner; Droop Monroe does the same with groups of n/(k + 1) voters. A rule satisfies an axiom if it always outputs an outcome providing it. Droop-JR requires that for every group of more than n/(k + 1) voters who all approve a common candidate, some voter in the group approves a member of the committee. The (Hare) Monroe rule satisfies Droop-JR when k divides n. Does it satisfy Droop-JR for all n and k?
literature.source_title: Justified Representation: From Hare to Droop
literature.location: Appendix, discussion before Proposition 3; Table 1, note d
literature.rationale: Proposition 3 of the source proves it when k divides n. Hare Monroe fails Droop-PJR even when k or k + 1 divides n, and Hare Greedy Monroe can fail Droop-JR depending on tie-breaking.

literature.title: Droop-PJR+ for the Droop Monroe rule
literature.statement: Approval-based committee elections with n voters and committee size k. The Hare Monroe rule assigns each winner a group of about n/k voters and maximizes the number of voters who approve their assigned winner; Droop Monroe does the same with groups of n/(k + 1) voters. A rule satisfies an axiom if it always outputs an outcome providing it. Droop-PJR+ is the Droop-quota version of the PJR+ axiom (groups of more than l n/(k + 1) voters with l commonly approved candidates must be represented, with the "+" strengthening that compares against any commonly approved unelected candidate). Droop Monroe satisfies Droop-PJR when k + 1 divides n. When k + 1 divides n, does Droop Monroe satisfy Droop-PJR+?
literature.source_title: Justified Representation: From Hare to Droop
literature.rationale: Droop Monroe and Droop Greedy Monroe satisfy Droop-PJR and even Droop-FPJR when k + 1 divides n (Theorem 4), and can violate them otherwise (Proposition 4).

literature.title: Droop-EJR+ and Droop-FJR for the Droop Monroe rule
literature.statement: Approval-based committee elections with n voters and committee size k. The Hare Monroe rule assigns each winner a group of about n/k voters and maximizes the number of voters who approve their assigned winner; Droop Monroe does the same with groups of n/(k + 1) voters. A rule satisfies an axiom if it always outputs an outcome providing it. Table 1 of the source leaves open whether Droop Monroe satisfies the Droop versions of EJR+ and FJR. Does every committee output by the Droop Monroe rule (in particular when k + 1 divides n) provide Droop-EJR+ and Droop-FJR?
literature.source_title: Justified Representation: From Hare to Droop
literature.location: Table 1 ("?" entries in the EJR+ and FJR columns for Droop Monroe); Conclusion
literature.rationale: PAV and Droop MES/EES satisfy Droop-EJR+ and Droop GCR satisfies Droop-FJR, so both axioms are satisfiable; for Droop Monroe the source has no positive or negative result.

literature.title: Does Droop-FJR imply BFJR in temporal voting?
literature.statement: Temporal approval voting: n voters, l rounds, one candidate chosen per round; voter i approves the set a_{i,r} in round r and her satisfaction is the number of rounds whose chosen candidate she approves. Droop-FJR (Definition A.6 of the source) and base full justified representation BFJR (Definition A.5, an FJR analogue from the general approval-voting model with feasibility constraints) are both defined there, and BFJR implies Droop-FJR (Proposition A.7). Does the converse hold, i.e. does every outcome providing Droop-FJR provide BFJR, possibly under some additional assumption such as no voter approving every candidate in a round?
literature.source_title: Strengthening Proportionality in Temporal Voting
literature.rationale: BFJR implies Droop-FJR (Proposition A.7). For the EJR analogues, Droop-EJR implies BEJR once no voter approves all candidates in some round (Proposition A.4).

literature.title: Uniqueness of equilibrium in the publication choice problem with many types
literature.statement: Researchers of types theta_1 < ... < theta_k with population densities mu_i choose publication amounts a_{i,j} >= 0 at venues j to maximize sum_j a_{i,j}^alpha v_j^beta (alpha in (0,1), beta > 1) subject to the budget sum_j c_{i,j} a_{i,j} <= 1; venue impact v_j is the average type of the papers published there. A pure-strategy equilibrium is a best-response profile consistent with the impacts it induces. Venue 1 is non-competitive: c_{i,1} is the same for all types. With more than two types, is the pure-strategy equilibrium always unique?
literature.source_title: The Publication Choice Problem
literature.rationale: The source states uniqueness for two types under a non-competitive venue (Theorem 4.1) and reports simulations with five types consistent with uniqueness (App. A.2).

literature.title: Can a static threshold be 1/2-robust under strategic reward signaling?
literature.statement: Prophet inequality with strategic players: each reward X_i ~ H_i belongs to a player who commits to a signaling scheme to maximize the chance of being selected; the searcher sees only the signals and uses a threshold stopping policy. A policy is alpha-robust if it is an alpha-approximation to E[max X_i] when players signal strategically (in equilibrium) and a 1/2-approximation in the standard non-strategic setting. Is there a static (single) threshold, possibly outside the usual spectrum of 1/2-approximate thresholds, that is 1/2-robust for every instance?
literature.source_title: Intrinsic Robustness of Prophet Inequality to Strategic Reward Signaling
literature.rationale: Thresholds in the standard 1/2-approximation spectrum are (1 - 1/e)/2-robust and no threshold in that spectrum does better in general (Theorem 4.1, Proposition 4.2); 1/2-robustness is achievable for i.i.d. and for log-concave rewards.

literature.title: Is the deterministic lower bound for finding minimal elements of a poset tight?
literature.statement: Given n elements of an unknown partial order of width at most w, accessible through a comparison oracle, a deterministic algorithm must output all minimal elements. The source proves that at least (w + 1)n/2 - w queries are needed in the worst case and that wn queries suffice. Is the lower bound tight, i.e. is the deterministic query complexity (w + 1)n/2 - w up to lower-order terms?
literature.source_title: Sorting and Selection in Posets
literature.location: Sec. 4 (introduction to the k-selection problem); Theorems 11 and 16
literature.rationale: Theorem 16 gives the adversary lower bound (w + 1)n/2 - w and Theorem 11 an algorithm with at most wn queries, so the leading constant is known only up to a factor of about 2.

literature.title: Linear-in-s approximation for pure equilibria of anonymous games
literature.statement: In an anonymous game with n players and s strategies, each player's payoff depends on her own strategy and on how many others play each strategy; payoffs are in [0, 1] and lambda-Lipschitz in that count vector. The source shows that a pure f(s) lambda-approximate Nash equilibrium always exists, with f quadratic in s, and that epsilon < lambda is impossible in general. Can the bound be improved to linear in s, and is s lambda a lower bound (some game has no pure epsilon-equilibrium for epsilon < s lambda)?
literature.source_title: Computing Equilibria in Anonymous Games
literature.location: Sec. 4 (Open Problems); also Sec. 1 ("We conjecture that the dependence on s can be improved to s lambda")
literature.rationale: Every lambda-Lipschitz anonymous game has a pure f(s) lambda-approximate equilibrium with f(s) quadratic in s (proof via Brouwer on an interpolated best-response map); matching pennies shows epsilon cannot go below lambda.

literature.title: Are strategyproof surjective facility-location mechanisms under scaling effects dictatorships?
literature.statement: One facility is placed at y in [0, 1]; agent i at x_i has cost d(x_i, y) q(y), where q is a continuous positive scaling function, so preferences need not be single-peaked. Are the deterministic mechanisms that are strategyproof and surjective (onto [0, 1]) under these preferences exactly the dictatorships?
literature.source_title: Facility Location Games with Scaling Effects
literature.rationale: For single-peaked preferences, strategyproof anonymous rules are the phantom-median mechanisms; for unrestricted preferences, strategyproof surjective rules are dictatorial. The source shows preferences stay single-peaked iff q(y) - |q'(y)| >= 0 wherever q is differentiable (Theorem 4).

literature.title: Best approximation ratio for temporal EFX under identical days
literature.statement: Goods arrive over rounds t = 1..T and are allocated irrevocably. An allocation sequence is alpha-TEFX if after every round the cumulative allocation is alpha-EFX: v_i(A_i) >= alpha v_i(A_j minus g) for all agents i, j and goods g in A_j. Under identical days the same multiset of goods (same values for every agent) arrives each round. What is the largest alpha such that an alpha-TEFX allocation always exists under identical days (for two agents, and in general)?
literature.source_title: Temporal Fair Division of Indivisible Goods with Structured Constraints
literature.location: Sec. 7 (Discussion and Future Works); Theorems 2 and 3
literature.rationale: Exact TEFX can fail under identical days when T > 2, even for two agents with identical valuations (Theorem 2); a 1/2-TEFX allocation exists and is computable in polynomial time for two agents (Theorem 3).

literature.title: Price of MNW for two agents
literature.statement: Two agents with additive, nonnegative valuations over indivisible goods, normalized so each values all goods at 1. The price of maximum Nash welfare (MNW) is the worst case, over instances, of the ratio between the optimal utilitarian welfare and the welfare of the best MNW allocation; the strong price uses the worst MNW allocation. The source shows both lie in [27/23, 5/4] for two agents. What are their exact values?
literature.source_title: The Price of Fairness for Indivisible Goods
literature.rationale: Theorem 5.4 of the source: for two agents the price and the strong price of MNW are at least 27/23 and at most 5/4. For general n the price of MNW is Theta(n).

literature.title: Linkedness and the two-agent price of connectivity
literature.statement: Goods are the vertices of a connected graph G; for two agents with an additive utility u, MMS(u, 2) is the best min-value over all bipartitions of the vertices and G-MMS(G, u, 2) the best over bipartitions into two connected parts. The price of connectivity PoC(G, 2) is the sup over u of MMS(u, 2)/G-MMS(G, u, 2). G is (a, b)-linked if for any disjoint vertex sets M_1, M_2 with |M_1| = a, |M_2| = b there are disjoint connected subgraphs containing them. For k >= 2, if G is (2, k - 1)-linked but not (2, k)-linked, is PoC(G, 2) = 2k/(2k - 1)?
literature.source_title: The Price of Connectivity in Fair Division
literature.rationale: Not being (2, k)-linked forces PoC(G, 2) >= 2k/(2k - 1) (Proposition 3.9). The case k = 2 holds (Corollary 3.6), and the conjecture holds for complete graphs minus a nonempty matching (Theorem 3.11).

literature.title: Quota and population monotonicity for four states at a common house size
literature.statement: An apportionment solution assigns, to every population vector of four states (all positive) and every house size h, a seat vector summing to h. Quota: each state gets the floor or ceiling of its standard quota h p_i / sum p. Population monotonicity forbids a state whose population weakly increases from losing a seat to a state whose population weakly decreases. Is there a deterministic solution for four states satisfying quota and population monotonicity when monotonicity is only required between profiles with the same house size (no anonymity, order preservation or other regularity assumed)?
literature.source_title: Quota and Population Monotonicity Across House Sizes are Incompatible for Apportionment to Four States
literature.rationale: Without order-preservation assumptions, quota and population monotonicity are incompatible for five states (arXiv:2202.11061) and for four states when comparisons may span house sizes (the source, using house sizes 3, 5, 8 and 10); for three states Webster's method is compatible with both.

literature.title: Linear entropy of geometric Plackett–Luce models
literature.statement: The Plackett–Luce model with weights w_1, ..., w_m draws a ranking of m alternatives by repeatedly picking the next alternative with probability proportional to its weight among those remaining. For the geometric weights w = (1, phi, ..., phi^(m-1)) with a constant phi, is the Shannon entropy of the resulting distribution over rankings O(m) for every phi in (0, 1)?
literature.source_title: Preference Elicitation as Average-Case Sorting
literature.rationale: Theorem 12 of the source proves entropy O(m) for phi in (0, 1/2]; its proof uses that removing entries does not increase the entropy of the weight vector, which needs phi <= 1/2.

literature.title: Is leximin among EF1 allocations Pareto optimal?
literature.statement: Indivisible goods, additive nonnegative valuations. Among all EF1 allocations (each agent envies another only up to removing one good from the other's bundle), choose one that is leximin-optimal: it maximizes the smallest utility, then the second smallest, and so on. Is such an allocation always Pareto optimal?
literature.source: The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare (ACM TEAC 7(3), 2019)
literature.source_title: The Unreasonable Fairness of Maximum Nash Welfare
literature.location: Appendix B (The Elusive Combination of EF1 and PO)
literature.rationale: Maximizing egalitarian welfare subject to EF1 need not be PO (a three-agent example in the source); MNW allocations are always EF1 and PO, and leximin refines the egalitarian solution in that example.

literature.title: Banzhaf veto distortion at simple majority with strict quota
literature.statement: Inverse power problem: given a target distribution m over players and quota q, choose voting weights whose p-propensity Banzhaf power is closest to m. The veto distortion of an instance is max{(1 - q) / (smallest m_i of a player who is a veto player under some optimal weights), 1}, and the veto distortion at quota q is its supremum over m. For q > 1/2 it is unbounded and for q = 1/2 with non-strict quota it equals 1. What is the veto distortion at q = 1/2 with strict quota (weights > 1/2 win); in particular, is it bounded?
literature.source: How Banzhaf Makes a Victor: Curing a Distortion Paradox in Weighted Voting (EC 2026)
literature.source_title: How Banzhaf Makes a Victor: Curing a Distortion Paradox in Weighted Voting
literature.rationale: Theorem 5.1: for every q in (1/2, 1) and every propensity p the veto distortion is unbounded; Theorem 5.2: with non-strict quota at q = 1/2 there is no distortion. For strict quota 1/2 the target (5/12, 5/12, 2/12) gives distortion at least 6/5.

literature.title: The Catch-Up conjecture
literature.statement: Catch-Up is played on a finite set S of positive integers: player 1 first removes one number; afterwards players alternate, and on a turn the mover keeps removing numbers (adding them to her score) until her score is at least the opponent's, staying strictly behind before her last pick; if she cannot catch up, she takes all remaining numbers and the game ends. Higher final score wins, equal scores draw. Is Catch-Up on {1, ..., N} a draw under optimal play exactly when N(N + 1)/2 is even (N = 0 or 3 mod 4)?
literature.source_title: Catch-Up: A Game in Which the Lead Alternates
literature.location: Sec. 3.1 (Optimal Play); Sec. 2.6 and Appendix 5.1 for the odd case
literature.rationale: When N(N + 1)/2 is odd no draw is possible, since the totals differ by an odd amount (proved in the source). For even N(N + 1)/2 the source computed optimal play up to N = 20 (all draws) and explored N = 23, 24, 27, 28 by Monte-Carlo tree search without contradiction.

literature.title: Complexity of width-2 ReLU verification
literature.statement: Let N : [0,1] → ℝ be a feedforward ReLU neural network with rational weights and biases where each hidden layer has width at most 2. Is the verification problem on [0,1]—deciding whether there exists x ∈ [0,1] such that N(x) = 0—NP-hard, or is it decidable in polynomial time? Concomitantly, is the discrete verification problem NP-hard: given such a width-2 network N and an integer n ≥ 1, deciding whether there exists x in DD_{1,3}^{(n)} := {∑_{i=1}^n a_i 4^{-i} : a_i ∈ {1,3}} such that N(x) = 0?
literature.source_title: Fractal Gadgets for Neural Networks: The Complexity of the Narrow Regime
literature.rationale: The paper shows that ReLU verification is polynomial-time solvable at width 1, NP-complete at width 3 on the discrete encoding set DD_{1,3}^{(n)}, and NP-complete at width 4 on [0,1]. Width 2 is conjectured NP-hard but remains open in both the discrete and continuous settings.

literature.title: NP-completeness of ReLU verification at width 3 on [0,1]
literature.statement: Is the verification problem for feedforward ReLU neural networks of width 3 on the unit interval [0,1] NP-complete? Specifically, given a network N : [0,1] → ℝ with rational weights and biases having at most 3 neurons per hidden layer, is deciding whether there exists x ∈ [0,1] such that N(x) = 0 NP-hard, or is it solvable in polynomial time?
literature.source_title: Fractal Gadgets for Neural Networks: The Complexity of the Narrow Regime
literature.rationale: The paper achieves NP-completeness on DD_{1,3}^{(n)} at width 3, but lifting the reduction to [0,1] requires width 4 to carry the fractal error register alongside the computation. The authors note that whether this lifting can be done at width 3 remains open.

literature.title: Polynomial-Time Approximate Nash Equilibria in Bimatrix Games with Error Below 0.3
